PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
"Trzls beats me," as the egg remarked when it
saw the spoon. THE plainest woman in the world may be passing fair—in a railway car. THE whip belongs to the most common variety

O f team stir. WIFE: "I don't see why women should not make as good swimmers as men.' Husband: "Yes—but you see a swimmer has to keep his mouth shut." As the course of true love never runs smooth, it is supposed that there will always be plenty of friction matches in the world. A CINCINNATI domestic has fallen heir to a fortune of 250,000 dollars. She has been invited to eat with the family. A BOY was asked what meekness was. He thought a moment, and said: "Meekness gives smooth answers to rough questions." "I WAS only footing one of your late Bills," re- marked a fond father to his daughter, after kicking her sweet William out of the front yard. " WHAT I want," cried an impetuous woman, struggling to reach a ribbon counter in a crowded store the other day—" what I want is free trade." AN impecunious fop said that his straitened circumstances were owing to his failure in the "yarn business ; " that is, nobody would believe his stories. _ _
MONEY and time are the heaviest burdens of life, and the unhappiest of all mort,ds are those who have more of either than they know how to use. . .

JOHNNIE, how rude of youl You hardly raised your cap at all when Miss Be'lisle passed, and she is always so nice to you. .Johnnie: That's just where it is, don't you know—when a girl's so partial to a man; if he pays her much attention she begins to think he's serious. AT a dinner party in Boston a young man from the West, who was visiting the host, was asked if he was fond of etymology. " Well, ye-es," he re- plied at a venture, "but I don't think I'll take any to-nig h t." Wily, you knock the breath out of me !" said the puffing forge bellows to a sturdy blacksmith. "Well, what oi it? You're the worst blower I ever tackled," replied the perspiring horse shoer. "No," said Miss Spinster, "I wouldn't have any fool of a man." "And as you cannot get any other kind," remarked Aunt Susan, "you prefer to remain single. Well, I don't know as I blame you." "Flow are you getting on now ?" asked a neigh- bour of Abraham Lincoln, shortly after Mr. L. had served the first term in Congress. "First rate, first rate, FIRST RATE," answered Lincoln, "ever since I stopped trying to run the whole world !"

" I WONDER," said a young lady, "why Hymep is alwvks represented as carrying a torch?' To which an Old bachelor sneeringly responded: " To indi- cate that he always makes it warm for people who marry." "OH, dear!" exclaimed Mrs. F., "where in the world did I put that reel of silk? I was very care- ful when I put it away to have it fixed in my mind where I placed it." "Had it fixed in your mind, did you?" replied Fogg; "but nevertheless you now seem to be mixed in your find." A PARISIAN paper says that "the first seventeen performances of Sardou's Crocodile have reaped the spkmdid harvest of 141,377 francs—an average of 8,01;() francs (f. 300 nightly.' That must be an extraordinary crocodile. We wonder where Sardou caught him! NEVER TOO LATE TO MEND.—At the French registrar's office a wedding party had been waiting a considerable time for the bridegroom. At last he came—an old man about seventy. "Another time," said the registrar, "try to be here a little sooner." _ _

"My dear madame," said a doctor to his patient, "1 am truly gratified to see you yet in life. At my last visit yesterday, you know I said you had hut six hours to live." "Yes, Doctor, you did ; but I did not take the dose you left me." " DoN r you think I look ?" inquired Mrs. Biasfolds, as she entered the room in a new brickdust red costume. Mrs. Biasfolds is what one might call decidedly plump; and, when Biasfolds calmly replied, "Yes, my dear, you look fat enough to kill, if that is what 3ou mean," it was not unnatural that Mrs. B. should flounce out of the apartment with a very flushed face and a quivering tongue. " AND that is silver ore, is it ?" said Mrs. Snaggs, as she exclaimed a piece of curious-looking mineral. "Yes, my dear," replied her husband. "And how do they get the silver out ?" "They smelt it." "Well, that's queer," she added, after apply- ing her nose to the ore; "I smelt it, too, but didn't get any silver." A FASTIDIOUS man who hated military trappings and the fussiness of milita officers, having declined to accept a commission of general in the militia, a wag remarked : "He declined to be general because he is particular." THE difficulty of expressing one's self in a foreign language is illustrated by the remark of a German girl who went to see a tine boy baby, and in en- deavouring to express her admiration, said: "Oh, my! what a nice fat ba.bee 1 How fat she is, don't her' MAMMA, explaining to her little girl, aged five, that everything she does and says is written down in a large book in heaven, the latter asks—" Are all the naughty things, too?" Mamma " Yes, dear." L. G. (pensively)—" Then I think I'll take a piece of indiarubber with me." Mx. LAMAN—" Why do you always question patients so closely about what they eat? Does the information you get help you to diagnose their cases?' Dr. Etude—" Oh, no! But by doing so I am enabled to guess what their station in life is, and how much fee I can probably get out of them." A HUSBAND who had incurred the anger of his wife a terrible virago, seeks refuge under the bed. "Come: out of that, you brigand, you rascal, you assassin!" screamed Ids gentle companion. "No, madam," he replied calmly, "I won't come out; I am going to show you that I shall do as I please in my own house !" "DEAR, dear," said a kind-hearted matron on meeting a friend whom she had not seen for a long time, "and you're not yet married, Jane, with your good looks, too ?" "No I'm not married yet," replied Jane with a laugh. "And how comes it that you are single ?" "Well," said Jane, with a twinkle of her eye, "I expect it's because I was born so." Wu r is a sheet of foolscap paper like a lazy young quadruped of the canine species? was the conundrum, and this was the answer: "In the first t place, a sheet of foolscap paper is an ink-lined (in- clined) plane; in the second place, an inclined plane is a slope up (slow pup), and there you see the resemblauce between a sheet of foolscap paper and a lazy young canine." AFTER the battle of Custozza a soldier, supposed to have been killed, was entered on the books of his company, "Died on the 24th June, 1866," &c. A few days afterwards it turned out that he was still alive, and the honest quartermaster made the fol- lowing entry—" Died by mistake." At length there came a letter from the Ministry of War announcing the death of the man at the hospital, when our sergeant recorded the fact as follows— " Realied, by order of the Ministry." AN English Lord who visited America was at a dinner given in his honour. A little daughter of his host who was too well bred to stare, but who eyed him covertly as the occasion presented itself, fins.' ly ventured to remark, "And you are really and truly an English Lord ? " " Yes, 'he answered, pleasantly, "really and truly." "I have often thought that I would like to see an English Lord," she went on, " and—and---' "And now you are satisfied at last?" he put in, laughingly. " No- no," replied the truthful little girl, "I'm not satisfied. I'm a good deal disappointed!" A COMMERCIAL TRAVELLER one day, at a country inn, was boasting somewhat extravagantly of the very extensive nature of the transactions in which he had the honour to be concerned. Amongst other proofs of the truth of his representations, he stated to his fellow-travellers that, "his house paid upwards of £3OO per annum for the article of writing-ink alone, to be used in their counting- house and other offices ? " " Oh!" replies a traveller in a different line of business, "that's a mere flea-bite to the business done by our house. Do you know," ha continued, that during the last twelve months we have saved, in that article alone, no leas a sum than £2,000, by merely omitting the dot's to our i's, and the crosses to our ts !" AEND (to a young mats): WII, out Num, I hear that your grandmother is dead." Young' man: " Yes ; she died yesterday." Friend : "It is the way of the world. We must all die some time, and the old lady was well advanced in years. She left a last will and testament, of course? I have understood she was wealthy." Young Man: "Oh, yes, she left a wilt and tt scament." Friend : "You were always a favourite of hers. Your name was mentioned, ot coat,el" Young Man: " Yes " and the tears began to stream down his cheeks), "my name was mentioned. I'm to have the testament,"

fordshire, draws attention to the curious fact that there has been a progressive increase in the rainfall in that county during the past half century. This phenomenon, however, is regarded by him as "a mere episode in a period of declining rainfall," and he warns us to look forward to a considerably re- &mot fall in the distant future, and to a lowerincf of the place of 'permanent saturation in the chalk of the Thames Basin from natural causes. The des- truction of forests and the lowering of the surface of the ground by sub-aerial denudation must,in Mr. IzTopkinson's opinion, tend to reduce the rainfall ; while this reduction, and the loss of water which must take place from its gradual percolation to a lower level owing to the cooling of the earth, must in time lower the surface and lessen the contents of the underground reservoir on which we now de- pend for a considerable portion of our water supply.

Dr. Dabbs, who has bsen so prominently before the world as Tennyson's doctor in his last illness, has written a new comedy, to which he has given the title of" Farewell." There would be something appropriate in the production just now of a work by Dr. Dabbs, and, if brought out promptly, "Fare- well " would be sure of a generally sympathetic first night audience, whatever its ultimate fate. Mr. F. J. Leslie has secured the piece.

On Sunday, the 23rd inst., the Sunday Lecture Society, of which Professor Huxley is President, begins a new series of Sunday afternoon lectures in St. George's Hall, Langharn place, at 4 p.m., when Dr. Andrew Wilson will lecture on "The Distribu- tion of Animals, and what it teaches." Lectures will subsequently be given by Mr. Wilmott Dixon, Prince Krapotkin, Mr. If. Brudenell Carter, Mr. Arthur W. Clayden, Professor H. Marshall Ward, and Dr. E. E.Klein.

Hans Nielsen, of Copenh agen,h as had the probably unique experience of being sentenced to death three times. Such is the lenity of Danish law, or, rather, the indisposition of the authorities to proceed to extreme measures, that this notorious criminal has already been reprieved twice and relegated to prison for a long term. It was in prison that he committed his last offence, for he murdered one of his gaolers. Nielsen began his career of crime at the age of eight by setting fire to a farmhouse, and it is doubtful whether he has ever earned an honest penny in the whole course of his existence. He was formerly resident in London. -- Speaking at the dinner given to Lord Roberts, at Simla, by the Royal Artillery, Lieutenant-General Brackenbury declared that the Corn mander-in- Chief has done more than any other man, past or present, in India, for the health, the comfort, the military training, and the physical and moral wel- fare of the private soldier, British and native. "I venture (he continued) to think that not the least of his pleasures will be the knowledge that he is beloved by every soldier; and that even now he prefers in his heart to the title of Lord Roberts of Kandahar and Waterford,' so worthily earned, that 1 other title which he has earned in camp from the ' affection of the soldiers—the title ot 'Bobs, God bless him!'"

It anyone steps on tea landlord's property he will be promptly summoned, but if a landlord ob- structs the public highway he is permitted to do so, ' and to repeat the offence with impunity. Mr. Scott-Jervis obstructed an old and much used road at Wallingford by placing a gate across it. The Highway Board removed it, but Mr. Scott-Jervis erected it again. Following the example of the Highway Board the inhabitants removed the new obstruction, but Mr. Scott-Jervis, who seems to be a particularly aggressive type of the grabber,put it up again. On Monday the Highway Bpard smashed the gate to atoms in the presence of the magis- trates. They ought to summon Mr. Scott-Jervis be- fore the magistrates.

An Irish journalist draws attention to the enor- mous difference between the prices paid to growers for fruit and flowers and those at which the middle- men sell them. A lady who said her rosebuds at a shilling the dozen saw them retailed at sixpence each, and another lady who was paid a shilling a iiiituire.! for her pears saw them on sale the same day at eighteenpence the dozen. At the same time, a resident of Dublin, who through the Press made a public offer to purchase garden produce at full market value, has received but one reply. It is to be suspected that the lion in the path of those im- poverished ladies who are anxious to sell their fruit and flowers is to be found in that fear of "anybody knowing " that is fatal to success in such cases.

The death of M. Henan makes a vacancy in the Academy, and already there is question in Paris amongst men of science and letters as to who shall succeed. M. Berthelot is certainly the favourite. His candidature was first seriously considered when M. Pasteur's illness threatened to leave his arm chair to be filled. It seemed so natural that one savant should succeed another, the greatest master of chemical science, by the greatest he left after him. The Academy elections have become pecu- liarly interesting lately on account of the persistent efforts of M. Zola's friends, and it is only fair to say that each occasion of the novelist's rejection has diminished his minority. Since M. &man's death M. Zola has himself announced that his candidature will be maintained "till the Academy wearies of him."

What one Revising Barrister considers legal another will not permit. On Thursday Mr. Mack- arness at Hammersmith, gave the vote to thirty- five policemen who were objected to by the Liberals on the ground that eight or nine of them slept in one room. " There was no sort of division in the ' room." In Clerkenwell the Revising Barrister re- fused to enfranchise about a hundred shop assist- ants because four or five of them slept in rooms in which there were no partitions. The cases aro similar even to the extent that it is the Liberals who suffer in botli instances, but both decisions nnot be legal. It would be worth while having the matter thrashed out inn higher court, were it not for the fact that these vexatious anomalies will be removed before long by the House of Com- mons.

:Ir. Ralph Dutton, the late chairman of the Lon- km and South Western Railway, was a burly, coin- fortabl--looking south-countly man, who loved a good dinner and a good story. Timshury Manor, Mr. Dutton's house,in the valley of the Hampshire Test, is rich in suggestions of his sporting tastes and his friendship with Lord Palmerston. No railway chairman came more in contact with distinguished people than Ralph Dutton. The Windsor branch alone brought him into contact with scores of cele- brities. He had stories to tell of the Sultan. the Czar, Napoleon, Garibaldi, and many more. There should be a chance of introducing these stories to a wider audience. Mr. Dutton kept a diary for forty- three years, and there should be material therein for a bright addition to the library of reminis- cences.

Mr. M. M. Trumbull. of Chicago. an able and energetic advocate of Free Trade in the States, has sent to his Free Trade friends in London advance copies of a new and enlarged edition of his book, "The Free Trade Struggle in England." It contains a fac-simile letter from the late Mr. John Bright, who wrote to Mr. Trumbull in 1882 : " The Ameri- can tariff is so incapable of defence that discussion of the strange burdens it lays upon your people can only end in some great change and great reform. Such a reform will bring our two great nations nearer together, but the advantage will prove to he much more for your people than for ours. . . In a few years after your tariff has been made reason- able it will be as easy to persuade the United States to go back to the times of slavery as to the days of the mischiefs of Protection."

In Berlin the other day a workman was boring a 1 hole in a wooden wall in order to put in a screw, when lie teceived a strong shock, and, ignorant of the cause, he left the gimlet in the hole and fled. At the same time the electric clock of the "Urania" opposite the house suddenly stopped, and the elec- tricians who managed the clock for a long time could not imagine what was the matter. The workman while boring had pierced the thin wooden wall and the lead covering of the electric cable which regu- lates the Urania clock, and at the same time slightly touched a" light-cable" with his gimlet. In this way a communication was established between the two cables, and the strong current from the" light- cable was led ir.to the clock cable, when proving fAr too strong for the clock it stepped the works. The clock company had provided for the protection of the cables, but had never thought of such an unexpected accident.

Lady Frederick Cavendish, whose paper at the laides' meeting of the Church Congress revealed a shocking tendency to intemperance among the women of the upper and middle classes, is a most delightful lecturer. Since the tragic death of Lord Frederick she has kept almost entirely aloof from society, but has taken an active part in philan- thropic work, and has frequently lectured at boys' clubs and similar gatherings. Lady Frederick is tall and slight, with smooth dark hair, dark eyes, regular features, and pale complexion. Her expres- sive face and clear, bell-like voice and a strong sense of humour make her very popular as a lecturer. With Mr. Gladstone his niece, Lady Frederick, is a great favourite, and during the alterations in his official residence at Downing-st. the fine house in Carlton House-terrace, left to her by her father-in-law, the late Duke of Devonshire, has been Mr. Gladstone's headquarters.

div.head: PARK BANDSTAND.
div.p: THE PARK BANDSTAND.
OPENING PROCEEDINGS.

On Saturday afternoon the new bandstand in Warrington rark, was foroaally opened, by the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Greenish). The weather was somewhat unfavourable, but the attendance was, I nevertheless, pretty large. Among those present, were the Mayoress, Councillors Bolton, Connell, Muir, Green, Hill, Smethurst, Hepherd, liutchinson, Y. Monks, Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Chorley (borough assistant), Longdin (borough surveyor) and Hunt (chief constable). Mr. J. T. Down's band was present, and prior to the com- mencement of the opening proceedings was photo- graphed, grouped round the bandstand, by Mr. T. Birtles. .

Councillor BOLTON said he had great pleasure, in inviting the Mayor to open, on behalf of the corporation, the new bandstand. (Applause.) The MAYOR said : It was with great pleasure that I accepted your invitation to perform this ceremony, namely, the declaring of this stand open. The Corpora- tion of Warrington, have erected this bandstand for the use and benefit of the inhabitants of the borough, hoping that it will be appreciated by all. In a manufacturing town we feel the benefit of a park like this, which was presented many years ago by our late generous fellow- townsmen, Lord Winimarleigh and Mr. George Crosfield. (Applause.) Every available attraction should be added so as to conduce still further to the pleasure and enjoy- ment of the inhabitants of Warrington ; and to listen to , good music in the open air, is without doubt, the most enjoyable and innocent recreation that a man or woman can have. (Hear, hear.) Before concluding. I must thank Mr. Down, who has come forward this afternoon with his excellent band to play us a selection of music, for the great interest he has evinced in the erection of this stand, his suggestions having been most valued by the Committee. I have great pleasure in declaring the stand open for the use and benefit of the people of NVarrington, and I hope that the music which is per- formed from it may be a great source of pleasure to all around, for many years to come. (Applause.) Councillor BOLTON said on behalf of the Corporation he had great pleasure in handing to the Mayor as a memento of that occasion and of his present year of office, an ink- stand and case. Mr. Bolton then, amidst applause, handed to his Worship a beautiful solid silver inkstand enclosed in a handsome case. The lid bore the arms of the borough, and was inscribed as follows :—Presented by the Corporation of Warrington to his Worship, the Mayor, Edward Greenall, Esq., J.P., on the occasion of his openintr the new bandstand in Bank Park on the Bth October, 1892." The Mayon said he thanked Councillor Bolton and the Corporation for so kindly presenting him with the gift, and it would be a matter of the greatest satis- faction to himself and his wife that they had one memento, something to show that in their efforts to do what they could for the benefit of the town they had been appreciated. The band afterwards nlayed " God save the Queen " on the stand ; and subsequently gave in most admirable style a selection of performances at the Drill Hall, which was crowded by an audience comprising all classes, who highly appreciated the excellent free treat afforded to I them.

div.head: PRINCESS AND HER SUN.
div.p: THE PRINCESS AND HER SUN.

A few years ago the Princess of Wales went to the tanle of the Holy Communion accompanied for the first time by her eldest son. She gave him that ! morning a little manuscript book containing texts and verses of hymns, which she had copied for him, " hoping," as she said afterwards," that they might help him to keep closer to the Cross." After his death, as she was stooping over him to lay some flowers on his breast, she saw upon a little table close to his bedside, the book, bearing marks of long and constant use. The rrincess told this fact to Canon Fleming, adding, with tears steaming from her eyes, "I could not but feel that Eddy had clung to the Cross." The woman who, in her grief, told the story of her dead boy, because she knew that all , other mothers would be glad with her, is the ! daughter, the wife, the mother of kings and princes. Yet the little worn book which gave her a hope that " Eddy had turned to the Cross "is of more value to her now than that proudest of earthly crowns, which he lost in dying.

div.head: ANCIENT BUT FOOLISH,
div.p: ANCIENT BUT FOOLISH,

A mediteval custom still prevails in Freiberg, in Breisgau. This is observed on the birthday of the reigning Grand Duke of Baden, and consists of a foolhardy trip to the topmost part ot the tower of the Minster. It is a dangerous enterprise, for the tower is 400 ft. high, and the ascent is made from the exterior of the building. The steeple-jacks in their ascent have to leap from stone to stone, often a yard apart, and one false step on the narrow ledges would be death. At the topmost pinnacle pistol-shots announce that the climbers have suc- ceeded. Then an immense gilded star revolves,and the descent is begun. Each man receives as a reward a sum of five marks from the State, and a sumptuous dinner. The other day, on the occasion of the sixty-sixth birthday pf the Grand Duke of Baden, three men undertook the ascent. One of them, on arriving at a projecting bar of iron half way up, went through an acrobatic performance. This was before an immense crowd of spectators. He twisted and twirled about :as if he were but within a few feet of the earth.

div.head: HOW AN EMPRESS'S JEWELS WERE
div.p: HOW AN EMPRESS'S JEWELS WERE
SOLD.

The following account of how the Empress Eugenie's jewels were turned into cash is given by Mr. W. Thorp in "The Still Life of the Middle Temple." An old friend of some thirty years' standing was returning home for his periodical change, when there met him at Bombay a telegram from one of the great European financial kings, briefly informing him that the Empress Eugenie was selling her jewels in hope of doing something to save the dynasty. A market for such costly things in such quantity was not to be found in Europe, leaving out of account publicity, which was not desirable, in view of a demur to be expected for many reasons from the Republic just born in the agonies of Sedan. But the native princes of India were always buyers of such jewels as these. the spoil of an empire ; the difficulty was to find a man of sufficient influence to approach them, with at the same time stamina, mental and physical, enough to carry some hundreds of thou- sands of pounds' worth over roan, rail, and river into territories where the Queen's writ runneth not, nor is the tramp of the constable heard in the land. In addition, the man must himself be trustworthy. Every preparation had been made for safety and secrecy ; the jewels had been taken to pieces, "jointed," so as to fold flat, and could be carried iii a leather belt worn round the body. My friend had the required qualifications, and accepted the task. Protected simply by a revolver, and with one trusty servant to accompany him, he assumed the belt, wore it on him night and day, waking and sleeping, and in the course of three months suc- ceeding in disposing of its contents, though his health suffered somewhat from the terrible anxiety and strain; for it is hard to say whether the dan- gers he ran were greater in or out of British terri- tory, by day or by night.

'iltie! 11.111, ll' 'IVA° Pt NI, !iztl THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 15, 1892.
DOWN 1Y THE SEA.

•1, , [WITIIOUT THE BASSINETTE.] BY JOHN PEERS. (Continued.) BRISTOL.—On landing in a strange city, alone, unfriended, and unknown—as a sea-borne waif— a species of human jetsom, there is a certain feeling of oneness—a kind of by-yoursellitude which is intensified by the fact of your having come over sea—as though you had landed among aliens. And this was so with me, although this was but a triendly visit of Lancaster to Glo'ster. In a strange town, rich in historic memories as this is, I have no objection to being lost—for a time—missing my way and finding myself among the strange and unaccustomed. By this way we may find things otherwise unfiniable of set purpose. Fancy, wandering down what appeared to be a common- sense, practical, everyday sort of street and finding it to be a vehicular eel de sae—terminating in what seemed to be an old church tower, with three Gothic archways—the two lesser side ones being termed "lanes," The one to the right, called Tower Lane, was, I expect, the shortest "lane " I ever was in. But alas ! when there is so much to see and so little time to see it ! It would never do thus to exhaust my time in search of Aust. As a prevent- ative of this catastrophe, I reluctantly brought myself to enquire of a stray policeman the distance and bearing of the museum. By virtue of "Robert's" direction, and the intervention of a passing tram ! wl.ich took me up one of the steepest inclines I ! have seen, I reached my destination in Bristol museum. Here, after a hurried glance at the treasures, locally collected —chiefly saurian remains—l again started, after certain sailing directions from Mr. Wilson, the Curator, by rail and road for Aust Cliff. First to a station rejoicing in the euphonious cog- nomen of Pilning. Here the porter, being asked ! the way to Aust, with a sweep of the arm indicated , a large angle of the horizon. Now, in this kind of direction, there are large possibilities of adventure, not to say misadventure. I rather like this kind of thing in a strange country ; nothing dogmatic about it, gives such large scope for the following of our own wayward fancies, by whose capricious leading, vs e see and learn so much, which might otherwise be unseen and unlearned ; thus we find "fresh woods and pastures new," cross roads and equally cross owners and occupiers. Who was the snarling misogynist who said that all the evils to which man is prone or liable may be traced back to—woman? Of course he traced back the proof of his wretched contention to that equally wretched Chaldan fable of the apple, the woman, and the man, in which the talking serpent plays such a conspicuous part. Ann, as conducive to further convineement in the matter, he points out that the historic accuracy of the latter member of the dramatis persona having been engaged in the part assigned him—that ever since he has used his belly as a means of locomotion. How he managed to get along before deponent sayeth not. This is a mere matter of detail which large-minded historians cannot stop to be bothered with. But lovely woman to be maligned in this way! to be connected —even in a fable—with a creeping, crawling, ear- wigging scaly "varmint "like that! It is a libel upon the" ministering angel" sex. Where, I ask, should we be were it not for the kind intervention of woman in the earlier stages of our existence? I answer, unhesitatingly," nowhere !" It is she who gives us eur first start in life—launches us from the blank shore of non-being upon the wide waters ! of the sea of life—to sink or to swim as fate and fortune and our own conduct shall determine. "No," I said, I will follow that good woman—who like myself has debarked at this funnily named station—and who even now is crossing a field to avoid a detour." "Would she kindly indicate the road to Aust?" "Certainly, the road she was going led there." But she would inquire at the house to which she was going, where they knew the neighbourhood well. "Oh! yes, straight on, couldn't miss it." Couldn't miss it! This may be set down as one of the few impossibilities which I have achieved. Certain it is I did miss it, and even now might have been wandering o'er the wilds of Glostershire had I not met a pair of drab leggings and a thick walking stick and implored the motive power thereof to put me once more in the paths of rectitude. The advice he proffered was that which would be so very valu- able in the affairs of life, if indeed it could only be followed there-"z-viz.: to begin again—to go back to the place from whence we started, and to be more circumspect as to the paths that lead our wander- ing steps astray. Go back to the station again! Here was a trial of my faith in the theory I have advanced—that the pinionless angel we call woman, who consents to abide with us in this vale of tears and to sweeten, lighten, and render endurable, its ills—l say it was a shock to my robust faith in the "fairness" of the sex to be thus misled by two of them, who, if they did not conspire, at least com- bined, to thus play upon my trustful ignorance. And to be put right again by that common creature, man! But, after all, perhaps these petticoared apteryx were only mistaken—thought they were right and knew no better. All owing to their bring- ing up! And their lack of one of the "Rights of woman "—a proper education; that kind of educa- tion—a leading out of the faculties—that makes more definite the otherwise hazy boundary be- tween what we actually know and that which we only think we know. But I have not time just now to enlarge upon this most interesting and suggestive theme. These con- founded rutty and ridgy cross-country roads are not favourable to philosophising on education— except as it applies to the road-maker—and he might tell us it is more the Want of material than the knowledge to apply it that he requires to enable him to mend his was. But it was a glorious walk • along this rough-bottomed country lane—which, I had elicited from my friend in the gaiters, would lead me eventually into the right road for Aust. The weather again was all could be wished, the vegetation on either hand showed that absence of the deteriorating hand of man,that is so pleasant in the truly rural districts, and last, but not least, I was in that state of health, without the salt and savouring of which all the other blessings of nature fall upon our jaded palatPs—insipid, unenjoyed. Bye-and-by this bye-lane ceased and brought me into a more frequented road, white with thickly lying dust. After some distance I again diverged into a lane leading among farms and orchards, and enlivened by satchelled urchins wending their way loquaciously to school. And the orchards, how pleasant to the eye, and how suggestive, to another sense, their golden burdens ! And the tree trunks, heavy with grey-lichen, were eloquent in their silent witness to the purity of the air. For here men do not arrogate to themselves the privilege of making their own atmosphere, as in Widnes, where the artificial cosmic envelope, in which we live, move, and have our being is equally eloquent, as to the evils wrought by man's " 'prentice hand" when tried in this business. Widnes, " Where wealth accumulates and men decay," physically, if not morally, with its life-destroying fog, almost per- petually aver-hanging, what a contrast it affords to the more happy coturtry lanes I am now treading, breathing a sweet and pure air, bearing only the Scents and sounds of nature's making! At last, after many windings, this country lane with its rustic sights and sounds gave place to a long level stretch of road along the edge of a salt marsh, with a salt sea smell and the subdued roar of brpking waters in harmony. therewith. At the far end of this level the road rose to surmount what I rightly took lobe the end and object', of my out- ward journey' :—Aust Cliff. Here I found an ancient and desolate hostelry, and jutting into the river—or into the beach, for the tide was out, an equally desolate stone jetty, both melancholy wit- nesses of more prosperous days.. Altogether, the place in its drear desertion reminded me of a some- what similar place in our river—lnca Opera—itself a disused ferry—as this is now the Old Passage— having given place to the New Passage—which again has had to succumb to the Severn Tunnel which dips beneath the water at this place and has taken to itself all the transit of both. But here is the Cliff of Aust showing its precipit- ous front to the river, into which, far out into the rapid current, it pushes its obtruding feet, here as tangle—and there as rapid-covered reefs. These reefs are, I should say, the mark and mea- sure of the denudation—cutting back of the cliff by the river. Anyway the process is still going or., the reefs are lengthening as the cliff recedes, under the combined influences of rain and frost. The general aspect of the cliff is much that of Laver- nook, of which it is supposed to be a continuation. Here again we see the red Keuper marls, followed , upward by the teagreen marls and black shales of Lthe Rlicetics. The noticeable difference is the 'greater thickness of the Keuper and the absence of the Lies limestone capping. Otherwise the two cliffs are much alike, and, indeed, are considered by geologists to be portions of the same formation— severed by the Severn—standing on opposite sides of the river :and distant some forty miles apart.

What vast possibilities of fossil-fin-ling this great riparian denudation suggests ! What volumes of instructive material old Father Severn has thus washed unregretfully to the sea ! But now, abandoning as idle these vain regrets as to what we may have thus lost, let us turn to the cliff, as affording more prospect of information. The black shales here are much higher and less acces- sible than at Lavernock. So I confined my atten- tion to the beach and its talus of fossiliferous debris. A. diligent though hurried search added to the quan- tity it not the quality of specimens already ob- tained. In the better developed Keuper, we have again our old acquaintance of Lavernock--the white gypsum band. Not only is this beautiful mineral shown in the cliff as before, but here it runs in fantastic patterns beneath our feet, in high contrast of colour to the red Keuper marls, which here form the beach. In one place, especially, was the outcrop of this alabaster very striking, viz., where it came out just at the foot of the cliff and lay upon the red marls, iii thick-ribbed water-worn masses, like a tide-rack. Its almost pertect similitude to the jetsam from a wrecked cotton ship was the idea suggested by its white and fleece-like foldings. . . .

I noticed that the country people in the neigh- bourhood had a fondness for this ornamental mineral for garden decoration. It, like the lime- stone chipping of our garden walks, retains its pristine whiteness, by its property of slowly weathering away from atmospheric influences. Both this—the sulphate—and limestone,the carbon- ate of lime, are slowly dissolved by rain water. Hence the surfaces of both these minerals are kept constantly clean and free from mossy growth, &c., which make both pleasant objects when contrasted by the gieen of surrounding vegetation. Now I had come to Aust with the intention of staying the night; but I had already done what was the object of my journey—obtained a few of the typical specimens of the formation—the useful ' rather than the rare and valuable being my aim— and considering that I had to be in Cardiff again next day—that I very much prefer sailing over , rather than tunneling under this fine river—the original plan of campaign was altered aud I was ordered back to Bristol via Pilning that evening. I found the walk back to the station much shorter, but not more interesting, than on the outward journey. Nevertheless I wished for a short spell of the Bassinette—without the sixteen incumbrances, or, better still, without all the " kids," except the sixteenth,who might be found useful in" shafting " the family coach—tor truly my well stored hand- bag seemed to grow heavier every added mile. But it may be accounted one of the greatest blessings of their life that all our wishes are not fulfilled for the asking. What, for instance, should I have done with the bassinette—hot to mention the sixteenth—when so much better a means of personal and impedimental conveyance was offered, and accepted ? " Clergy- man of the Church of England, I presume ?" said the farmer from the trap. " Get in, and ride with me as far as our roads lie together ; I'm true blue, myself." Disclaiming the imputed honour, thus bestowed upon so dissident a layman, and not stopping to inquire as to the nat Lire and quality of his" true blue 'ism, I stepped into the trap, and jogged along with my hearty friend until a turn in the road separated us, with mutual good wishes and a genial invitation on his part, to visit him when next in that neighbourhood, I alighted and very shortly found myself awaiting the Bristol train at Pilning. Yes ! awaiting the tardy advent of a too-too dilatory train at a roadside station.

Now. I have known people who have stamped I and raged, and made imprecatory remarks upon the I unkind fates that thus consigned them to such distasteful delay. Wrong! very wrong of them ! For in this giving way to the impetuoAities of their I unsaintly tempers what great opportunities of } spiritual enlightment and improvement are thereby lost to them ! But I am afraid they regard this detention as an unmitigated evil rather than a grand opportunity for spirit-chastening. And how thankful we ought to feel to that body of tenevol- ents who take such care to provide us with conso- lation in this our affliction by hanging 'Scripture Texts" conspicuously on the walls! What a solace in our sad and solitary situation to be able to turn to Job and to read the record of his patience in affliction (not forgetting to deplore the spiritual darkness of the unregenerate who, in pencil, has interlined the text with the remark that "Job never was in this confounded hole !") And then the hope of deliverance from this place of probation, which may be drawn from the text as to the sure and certain hope of a joyful resurrection! For are we not here as the dead and buried, hoping for deliverance? And then what instruction may be derived from the perusal 'of the pencilled observa- tions of the pietist who asks questions and pro- pounds unanswerable conundrums upon the ground glass window-pane! The query "Where wilt thou be in eternity ?" does not affect me so much as the question " How shall I, both for the benefit of my- self and others, spend the time allotted to me here ?" And, in my opinion, the advice" Prepare to meet thy God" might very well be supplemented by the advice "Prepare to meet thy creditors." The latter Ncould be an excellent preparation for the first, the meeting taking the form of prompt pay- ment of first bills, and an avoidance of that dam- able iteration—" to account rendered," How mis- erable the fate of those who so often are in receipt of this phrase, if they themselves have to render an account of it! And doubly great is this iniquity in those who are set to teach the people to "Render unto Cmsar that which is Cmsar's," which, of course, applies equally to the subjects of Cmsar, as to Cassar himself. To keep back duly earned money is a robbery to the extent of the retention. The clergy are great, sinners in this way—more, I dare say, from want Of thought and business habits. But that species of commercial hypocrisy which consists in a strict attendance at church or chapel in unpaid for finery—in great display and the con- stant receipt of "duns "—should meet with the con- demnation it deserves, and those who practice it, well-merited contempt. It may '-se all very well to "prepare a mansion in the skies," but this should not be done by depriving your tradesmen of that by which they may keep the house door open, and the wolf—in the shape of tax and other collectors— from it! Let our cry be less cent and more dis- count! But hark! here is relief in the form of Stephen- son's Horse newly emerged from the Severn Tunnel. So 1 unregretfully leave " Job " to his lamentations and his comforters, and am at last spirited away from this place of desolation, and after a change and another awaiting—without "Job" this time—l ' was again safely set down in Bristol. (To be continued.)

div.head: TENNYSON INCIDENT.
div.p: A TENNYSON INCIDENT.

A quotation regarding Lord Tennyson made in "The Daily News" last week from Sir Henry Tay- lor's correspondence showed that in 18.52 the poet was staying at Reading or its vicinity. Upon this "The Reading Observer" makes the following note: —"The question naturally arises as to whom Tennyson was visiting in this locality on the occa- sion under notice. We had thought it must be Miss Mitford at Three-Mile-Cross, but on searching that eminent authoress's published letters we came upon a reference which while suggesting a clue as to where the poet stayed leaves little doubt that it was not with Miss Mitford Writing from Three-Mile-Cross on December 160, 1849, to Mrs. Browning, Miss Mitford says :--1 All the world is publishing. Alfred Tennyson says that people now-a-days are not merely indifferent to poetry—that they absolutely hate it. I heard this from a sweet young woman (Mary Repton, daughter of one ot the Prebendaries of Westminster) who is staying close by, at Mrs. Anderdon's, and has taken to me as young people sotnetimesdo. She is intimate, very, with all the Tennysons, and speaks of them more highly than I ever heard anyone; perhaps she knows them better She says that they are the nact unworldly people she ever knew, valuing everybody by .their personal qualities, apart from all considerations of rank or wealth or fame or consideration. Indolence is the besetting sin of the race ; but they can work if they will. For instance, she made Alfred dig up the whole garden at her fathers country living near Seven- oaks ; and he did it capitally.' . . . Another interesting circumstance connects Tennyson with this district, as he was married at Shipla.ke Church, in 1817, to MissErnily Sellwood, a lady from his native county of Lincolnshire, and who survives him."

div.head: PRIDE OF THE MILL
div.p: PRIDE OF THE MILL
, A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BT LAlhtc :TEAN LIDBEY, CHAPTER XXI.
"WE ARE SO SAD -MY HEART AND I. Yea, it was a strange betrothal, intense love on one side, kindly liking4the result of pity—on the other.

John Rochester was well pleased over it. Hilda Rochester alone was grave. She had pon- dered long and earnestly over the matter when she heard of it. "Could it be possible that he has learned to for- get that other love 2" she asked herself in wonder. "And his heart has gone out to Elaine in the re- bound 7" She had heard of such things.

As long as Arthur did not- come to her of his own free will and make a confidant of her, she would not broach the subject to* him save to con- gratulate him. She could see, too, that he did not look happy. In the midst of their hurried preparations for the wedding and the journey a cable dispatch was received, asking John Rochester to come in person to attend to the European business, as a complication of affairs had arisen which would require it. Thus it was the hasty marriage which was to take place that week was postponed, Elaine declar- ing she would take her time now to prepare for an elaborate wedding. Three months from that time was accordingly set for the event to take place. Patrice, Elaine's trusty little maid, heard of the arrangement with a thoughtful face. "I hope you won't take no offence if I speak my mind, Miss Elaine, and that is, I am sorry to bear that wedding is postponed," she said, shak- ing her head dubiously. "It isn't lucky, people say." , Elaine laughed a gay', bright, happy laugh. "That is all nonsense, Patrice," she said. P Peo- ple should not, be superstitious. I shall marry Arthur Rochester, unless .he or I should die before the time set for my wedding. Have no fears on that score, my good girl." "I once lived with a young lady who said the same thing when her marriage with her lover was postponed," replied Patrice, "and when the day came at last, the feast was ready, so was the bride elect; but the bridegroom was missing. It broke her heart, Miss Elaine, and two days later they buried her in her bridal robes, poor, pretty lady; death was her bridegroom." "I do not like to hear such dolef al stories," cried Elaine; impatiently. "Thank goodness, I am not superstitious. The engagement was duly announced, and mat- ters went on smoothly enough. •' There were times when Elaine did wish that her lover was less cold: but, then, she reasoned with herself, some gentlemen were more demonstrative than others. One evening she 'entered the library and found Arthur sitting at his desk, his face white as death, reading intently a paper which fairly trembled in his grasp, his hands shook so. With a gleam of girlish mischief in her eyes (for she had not as yet caught a glimpse of his face, for his back was toward her), Elaine stole lightly into the room and came up behind him, wondering if some subtle instinct would warn him of her near presence; but no; he was too deeply engrossed in his paper for that. Peering cautiously over his shoulder, Elaine pro- ceeded to examine amusedly the columns in which her lover was so absorbed. Her eyes ran down one item after another. "Surely there was nothing on the whole page Of special interest," she told herself. Lightly enough her eyes bad glanced over the lines that held Arthur Rochester spell-bound. There were but a few sentences, and read as follows : "The friends of Colonel Whitney, the well-known millionaire mill-owner of Pittsburgh, will be glad to learn that he and his charming and accomplished niece, Miss lenie Lawrence, will ,•onn take up their resider.c permanently at No. L,xing.on Avenue. The yung lady will be a valuable acquisition to New York society." And directly beneath this was the formal an- nouncement of lorries engageinvart to Mr. Frank Lyons. ,

The words seemed to stand out on the page be- fore him in letters of fire. -Arthur had told himself over and over again that he was (1-ad to all emotion—that the old love was dead in Li, lie:at—tLat it had been slain by the falserie,s, if tl,o girl he had loved but too well; yet as be read tbi., his love so long repressed, his anger so long kept down, rose in a hot, passionate torrent. He was like one bereft of reason. That mighty love which he had t..elieved dead surged again through his heart and soul. It mastered him again, and while he vowed to himsel that be abhorred' her, he couid have kissed the ground at her feet. He had never loved lonia more madly, more wildly, than now, when he knew that she was soon to marry another. He loved, yet hated her; he ciin.-ed, yet blessed her; he was mad with in eer, yet mad with love. He was to be pitied if ever a man was. Why should he care 7 he muttered, clenching the paper tightly in his hand. ' He had found her as false as Judas. Yet, even though he said that, he was torn with different emotions. Love, jealousy, anger swayed him. alternately. She was coming to New York. If he went into society he must meet her sooner or later—must look into the face of his false, fickle love, who was lost to him forever. Never again while the sun shone or the sea rolled —never while the blue heavens stretched out above him, would she, the girl whom he loved so dearly, be anything to him again. He had looked in her face, held her hand for the last time. Lost to him! and as the words went home to his heart, like a dagger's thrust, he groaned aloud. "Arthur, what is the matter? Are you ill, dear?" A little lily-white hand had crept into his own. Elaine's lovely, anxious face was bending over him. He recovered himself by a strenuous effort. A forced laugh fell from his lips; but it was accom- panied by a shudder. "Ill? Why, no, Elaine. I was only engrossed ia my thoughts." , "They could not have been very pleasant ones, ' Arthur, judging from your face," she said, anxiously. "If you have any trouble," she went on, wistfully. "you should share it with me." "But I have no troubles, as you phrase it, Elaine," he answered, lightly. No matter what he himself suffered, he thought, Elaine's life should not be clouded by that dark past. "I had almost forgotten the object for which I came in search of you, Arthur,* she said at length. "You asked me to let you know if I intended to accept Mrs. Tresham's invitation to her ball on the 20th. I think I will, Arthur. I have heard that it Is to be given in honour of a new debutante in New York society. I have forgotten the name." "As you please, Elaine," said Arthur, wearily. "These affairs rather bore me; but if you enjoy ' them, I shall be very pleased to take you. When is It to be?" he asked again, looking thoughtfully at the lovely, animated face. "On the twentieth," Elaine responded. A few days later a similar scene was being en- acted in a lovely blue and gold boudoir of a Lexing- ton Avenue mansion, which was now the home of Colonel Whitney arid lonie. Miss Carriscourt had accompanied them, and on 1 this particular morning there had been a lively dis- cussion between that lady and lonic over an open 'letter which lay in the girl's lap. "Why should you wish to hold aloof from society, my dear?" said Miss Carriscourt, laying a white hand on the girl's curly head, "I assure you it would not be right. As Colonel Whitney's heiress, it is positively expect( dof you. Mrs. Tresham is very kind to give a ball in your honour. You must go, my dear. You cannot be rude." lonie raised a lovely pair of dark eyes, heavy with unshed tears, to her companion's face. "I feel as though I never cared to dance again I" Miss Carriscourt looked earnestly into the beauti- ful face. "Do you know you are sadly changed, lonie, since you sent Arthur Rochester from you 7" she said, slowly. "I often question whether or not you are really happy new—if you really care for the lover you are soon to wed now in Arthur's stead." "I made the choice of my own free will," ex- claimed lonie, with a piteous attempt at reckless gayety. "Why, then, should you doubt it 7" "You are growing so cold and proud, even with sue, dear," replied her companion, slowly. "I am afraid all is not as it should be. Make a confidant of me, lonie. Let me help you in your love affairs. Even in these a young girl often needs counsel. Tell me, dear, have you and Arthur quarrelled? Did you send him away, and through pique en-
It i 8 not a dye.

required to do the work. There should not be a vested interest in the shape of a fO3 for which no equivalent was performed. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON in replying, said that the com- mittee did not think it was right to continue to pay to a person fees for which he -did nothing. (Hear, hear.) They were, there-fore; determined to try the experinteric which they hoped would be successful, and. compel .the sexton to do the work himself ; and then he would take the fees. In answer to Councillor Green, the Alderman 'said that, provided any resident in St. Paul's died and was buried in consecrated ground, the sexon was entitled to be paid a shilling, but if the interment took place in unconsecrated ground he would get nothing: ,The niinutes were then carried.

div.head: OAS COMMITTEE.
div.p: OAS COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended —" That the Gas Engineer be allowed when sent out of town for the night, expenses similar to those allowed to the Town Clerk. That plant be erected at the Longford Works for distil- ling tar, and that Mr. Haydock be instructed to obtain tenders for the neces4ary plant. Councillor R. FAIRCLOUGH proplsed the adoption.

Alderman WRIGHT seconded. Councillor BotroN asked the reason of the recommen- dation as to the Gas Engineer's expenses, and said he should propose an amendment unless he got an explana- tion. Councillor DIXON said he supposed the Council would have an estimate placed befere them as to the plant for distilling tar before the matter w vs finally confirmed. Councillor R. FAIRCLOIIGH said the tenders would come before the Council. _ _ _ _

CounciUor BuicirmunsT : I think before you do pur- chase them it should be laid before the Council for approval. You will not purchase the plant and then come to ask for permission after, though I know you do &little of that every now and then. Councillor R. FAIRCLOUGH, answering Mr. Bolton's question, said Mr. Craddock was charging certain ex- penses, and the cornattee would rather that these were defined, and that was the reason for the recommenda- tion. _ _ .

Alderman CHANDLEY : Are the Gas Committee bound to give a quotation of their tenders to this Council before acceptance? Counellior BUMPIEST No, I don't say before accept- ing. I said before purchase. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: FIRE ENGINE COMMITTER.
div.p: FIRE ENGINE COMMITTER.

This Committee recommended that the wages of Mr. Thomas Ratcliffe, the engineer, be increased to 355, per week. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Councillor HUTCHINSON, seconded by Councillor &au- nt:MST. $

div.head: WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: WATER COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended :—That the tender of the Glenneld Company, Limited, of Kilmarnock, for the supply of the following goods be accepted :-35 4- inch diameter spindle hydrants, at 19s. di. each. 15 2i-inch diameter spindle hydrants, at 17s. 81. each. 50 surface boxes, at Bs. each. The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Council- lor 11111.111 RD.

div.head: GENERAL PURPCAFS COMMITTEE. THE PROPOSED LATCHFORD RECREATION GROUND.
div.p: GENERAL PURPCAFS COMMITTEE. THE PROPOSED LATCHFORD RECREATION GROUND.

The minutes of this Committee reported :—The Com- mittee considered the question of couverting St. James's Old Burial Ground into a Recreation Ground, and were of opinion that the only practicable use that could be made of it was to cover in and asphalt the whole of the surface of the ground, after the removal of the grave stones; and tbat there would be no utility in laying out the ground in ornamental walks and flower beds. The Committee recommended that the common seal of the borough be affixed to the following documents: Mort- gages of the Water Undertaking for £9OO ,• the Gas Undertaking for £2,300 ; and the Water Undertaking (re-issue), £250; agreement with the Longford Wire, Iron, and Steel Co., Limited, as to easement for Gas Pipes; agreement with the Haybridge Iron Co., Limited, for tenancy of Hope Hospital; agreement with Mr. Murray Douglas as to the purchase of a strip of land at Bank Quay and Factory-lane. The Cmitazgan moved the adoption ot the minutes, with the exception of that as to St.Jamea's burial ground, and that it be referred back. Alderman CHANDLET seconded. He said he had had a conversation with the vicar of St. James's, and he hoped the Council would not consider this question was finally disposed of. The General Purposes Committee thought it would be possible to cover the whole of the burial ground with asphalt. The vicar and also the patron of the living thought that a middle course might be arrived at, and that there could be a bed in the middle and borders round. That would not, practically be arranging for flower beds, and walks, which would be quite out of character in a neighbourhood of that kind. He did not think it would be necessary to withdraw the minute in order to prevent anything being done. Mr. R. FAincLouon said there had been a good many meetings about open spaces. They had not the monet to provide these places, and this was the only little bit of work they had done in this way during the last two years, and if the resolution were passed as it was the whole of the work would be thrown away, because if they could not get the ground given surely to goodness they were not going to buy it. Alderman Surron That resolution is nothing.
Alderman CHANDLEY : What I mean to say is that the question will be re-opened with the Vicar, from what he said. _ .

Councillor R. FAIRCLOUGH proposed that the minute be withdrawn. Councillor FLOOD asked the Town Clerk whether a certain area of space was required before it could be adopted under the Act of Parliament as a local space by a public body. The Towts CLRRIC replied that there was no such restriction.

Councillor BOLTON said the Committee felt thov should like to have the ground as an °pm space, but the con- tingencies were so much, and it was going to cost as much as to buy an open space and lay it out. If it were laid out in flower beds there would have to be a caretaker appointed. They wanted an open space, or something that could be used as a recreation ground for the people, at the least cost to the ratepayers and with the greatest benefit to the public. There were legal difficulties in the matter of faculties and that sort of thing, and it was thought better to let the matter stand over until an opportunity turned up of making a better bargain. There would be nothing gained by withdrawing the minute, as the Committee simply said there would be no utility ie laying out the ground. Alderman Surrota, supported the proposal to leave out the minute, remarking that if the Committee re- considered the matter, and made a further appeal to the vicar of St. James's, and some explanations along with it there would be a disposition to lot them have the ground on the terms desired. Councilbr Bovroir : That is all we want. The minutes were adopted, with the omission of that discussed.

div.head: COUNCILLOR HILL'S MOTION.
div.p: COUNCILLOR HILL'S MOTION.

Councillor HILL rose to propose the following motion : —" That any new street paved and formed by the Cor- poration or to their order, the owners of property front- ing or abutting on the street shall be allowed 7 years to pay for the same, either in 7 yearly instalments or at the end of 7 years, at the option of the property owner% and 4 per cent, for the money till such time it is paid." Councillor BEPIIERD asked the Town Clerk if the motion was in order.
The Town CLERK replied that it was not, and if it were passed it would have no binding effect upon the Council.
Alderman SurroN : It is no use discussing it, then.

Councillor HILL asked the Town Clerk why the motion was not in order, as there were plenty of other towns that had adopted the principle, and this being the case, he did not see why it could not be adopted in War- rington. The Town CLERK : The resolution cannot be adopted in this form. If the Council were of opinion that it was desirable to allow time to owners for the payment of private street expenses, then they would have to pass a resolution for each separate street, declaring the expenses to be private improvement expenses. Councillor ROBERTS took it that all the Council could do was to make a recommendation, involving the principle of the resolution. Councillor HILL said one reason why he bad brought it before the Council was that there was a resolution some time ago that the Council should adopt the Private Street Act, which gave powers to the Corperation to borrow money and to charge interest to the builders upon the money invested in paving the streets. If the Council adopted that Act and got powers to borrow under it his resolution would then be in perfect order. He gave notice of motion that in case the Act were adopted, this matter should be considered.

. . The TowN CLERK said a motion approving of the general principle, without specifying the number of years would be in order now, but even if passed would not bind a future Council. In reply to Mr. Mum, the Town Clerk said seven years was a period in excess of the terms allowed in other towns.

div.head: SANITARY COMMITTEE'S PRESSURE OF WORK.
div.p: THE SANITARY COMMITTEE'S PRESSURE OF WORK.

Councillor H. ROBERTS, in accordance with notice, proposed the following motion That the duties and responsibilities devolved upon the Sanitary Committee having, from various causes, considerably increased, it is desirable at an early date, to take such steps as will provide for the division of such duties and responsibili- ties, and as will place the same under the control and supervision of two separate Committees." Councillor Roberts said it was not his intention that evening to take up the attention of the Council long. He bel.eved that the discussion at the last meeting of the council had somewhat cleared the atmosphere—(The Mayor : I hope so)—on one or two debatable points. He regretted the absence of the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, and that regret was heightened by the fact of the cause of his absence. No one regretted more than he did that Alderman Burgess should be indisposed. As a sort of preface to what he had to say that night, he might say that he was only carrying out a view which he had held for the past twelve months. He had advocated the principle contained in his resolution at the Council meetings, and more than once in the Sanitary Commit-

tee. It was because he felt that the interests of War- ringtnn urgently demanded an addition of strength to the ins naereneet of sanitary affairs—by wheel term he • ineludiel the whole question of sanitary matters—that I he brought the subject forward, in the hope that the Council would'adopt the recommendation practically ' coritAtned in the resolution which he-siatnnitted:- Itreire first place, he thought that everybody who was a member of the Sanitary Committee, or who had been a member of the Sanitary Committee, would admit that the Committee had been for years considerably overworked. They met every Wed- nesday night, and as a rule the business occupied rarely less than an hour, very frequently indeed two hours, and not unfrequently three hours. A% a result a considerable amount of work which required careful consideration had to be rushed through somewhat hur- riedly in the latter portion of the time that the Commit- tee dented te business. That was net at all desirable. Apart from that, the work connected with sanitary matters in Warrington had become so divers in charac- ter that there were at least two natural divisions in that work which suggested themselves at once to any person who was acquainted with it. In the first place, he considered that they might very properly place the control of the Longford Works and the Intercepting Depots under a separate Committee. The 'capital un- paid at present in connection with Longford and the depots was nearly £23,000, and the expenditure last year upon those departments which included the scav- enging of the streets, collection of nightsnil, which were part and parcel of the Sanitary Committee, was over £9,000. Such being the case, he thought that it would be admitted at once that the control of such large sums as he had mentioned, and work of such diverse nature and of so important a character, ought to be entrusted to a separate committee. In addition to a Sanitary Works Committee, he thought the town needed a Health Committee pure and simple. (Hear, hear.) He would suggest that that Committee should have the entire management of the hospital, and everything appertain- ing to the treatment of infectious diseases and the administration of certain Acts of Parliament which the Committee, as a whole, were at present charged with. It would perhaps be a surprise to the Council to learn that the Sanitary Committee had to administer no fewer than 17 Acts of Parliament, namely, the Contagious Direases (Animals) Act, 1878 to 1890,the Animals Order, 1886, the Dairies,. Cowsheds and Milkshops Order, of 1885 and 1886, the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879. The Sale of Food and I Drugs Acts,lB7s and 1879, The Canal Boats Acts, 1877 and 1884, The Quarry (Fencing) Act, 1888, The Marga- rine Act, 1887, The Sale of Horseflesh, &c, Regulation Act, 1889. The Infectious Disease (Prevention) Act, 1890, The Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1890,1 The Factory and Workshops Act, 1891, the Public Health Acts, 1875, 1889, 1891. The Infectious Disease (Notifi- cation) Act, 1889, The Towns Police Clauses Act, 1889.1 The Rivers Pollution Prevention Act, 1876. Be thought' that the mere recitation of the labour involved in the administration of 17 Acts of Parliament was in itself, sufficient evidence of the necessity of a separate com- mittee being appointed to deal with the administration of all matters appertaining to the public health referred to—the hospital and the administration of these 17 Acts. The fact was at present the Acts were only very partially administered. Although he had been a mem- ber of the Sanitary Committee several years, he was absolutely unaware that the administration of all these Acts lay in the province of the committee. He did not profess to be acquainted with one-third of them or even the principles they involved. There was a very old axiom well understoed everywhere by business men, that if too mush was placed on a man or a com- munity something was bound to be shirked. He was speaking in all honesty as a mem- ber of a Sanitary Committee, and as one who was prepared to assume his part of the responsibility of anything which was to be shared. He did not wish to blame the chairman of the committee, or anyone connected with it. He brought the question to the Council, treating it as a court of appeal, and in the Interests of Warrington, asked whether it was not time that the whole question should be reconsidered with a view to discussing whether it would not be advisable to have a fair division of labour, which would have for its object and result better management of sanitary matters in the town. Everyone knew that the condition of health in Warrington was very unsatisfactory. He did not wish to go into debatable matter in regard to the cause of it that day, but he did think the time was coming when the Sanitary Committee would have to con- sider the pail system. And then if they did not decide to depart from the system in vogue, they would cer- tainly have to do something in regard to the dis- infection of the material which was conveyed through the town in vans which were not easy to describe. (Councillor Dixon : Hear, hear.) There was another point to which he wished to refer, and that was the question of the insanitary area, which had been dwelt upon by the Medical Officer of Health, as far back as May last, and in April this year, and on another occa- sion. It was a matter which required very early consid- eration. They could not afford to goon as at the present, with a district in their midst with a death rate of over 40 perl thousand, constantly breeding disease, and those infectious diseases which the Council so much desired to remove would not be removed until the elements of the mischief had been dealt with. He was surprised to learn that there were 391 houses in Warrington on the list stated to be without separate closets. That was a condition of things which ought not to obtain a moment longer than avoidable. All this was simply the result of overwork on the part of the committee. The fact was that the manipulation and the eternal discussion of Long- ford had taken up so much time that there was very little time left for the discussion of other subjects_ (Cries of " hear, hear.") He thought it was admitted by all the members of the Council that 20 years ago the committee was capable of dea'inu with the sanitary affairs of Warrington because sanitary reform was then only in its infancy. The population had increased so much, and there had been such an enormous growth of sanitary legislation, that he thought the time had come when both on financial grounds and on crounds of public health—because the two went together since you could not have a financially prosperous town in an unhealthy Icondition—and seeing that so much capital had been in- vested at Longford and on the depots and so much was being expended year by year, when these departments should be under a separate committee on the one hand, and a health committee should be formed to have the administration of the Acts of Parliament and the control of matters pertaining to infectious disease. This would result in a very great improvement and sanitary reform in Warrington, and prove a great relief to the Council and a great boon to the ratepayers at large. Councillor FLoon seconded the motion. He had long since come to the conclusion that the committees was overburdened with work, and had often felt that the officials in connection with the committee had work to do that completely paralysed their efforts to do justice to the objects they had in view. Everybody must feel that the condition of the sewers was most unsatisfac- tory, and repeatedly it had been brought to the attention of the committee that this would probably cause a large amount of disease. The drainage in the area where disease principally existed was thoroughly bad, and the bad system of inspection there brought bad results in its train.

Alderman PIA= endorsed Mr. Roberts's remarks. Alderman Sorrow expressed surprise that Councillor Roberts had not brought the matter before the Sanitary Committee. Re believed that if he did he would be

,ipported hY nearly every memher of that committee. —(A Councillor : Except the Chairman.) It did not natter .Ibour he Chairman. If there was a majority in favour of any schem i would be submitted to the Ccuiriil for anproval. Such being the case, he was at a loss to know why the motion had been brought before the Council that evening. r,f. proper authority to deal. with the question of the suh-divishn of labour was the Sanitary Committee. (" No, no.") They knew their oWn deficiencies far better than any members of the Council. _ .

Councillor FLOOD : This question was opposed at the committee meeting. Councillor BOLTON supported the motion. If the sub- ject had been dealt with at a committee meeting, it would have been referred to a sub-committee, which would never have been called together. (Laugher.) They had had enough of sub-committees. He was sorry that the Sanitary Committee was not satisfied with the work of the officials. He was under the impression that their work was done in a satisfactory manner. Councillor FLOOD : They are not able to do it.

Councillor BOLTON said that he considered that the Sanitary Committee had passed a vote of censure on themselves. If they were unable to have the work performed properly, they should have engaged more officials. _

....... Alderman CHANDLEY agreed with Alderman Sutton's remarks. He believed that in the plenitude ol counsel- lors there was wisdom, and that large committees were better. H disagreed with the statement that the town of Warrington was most unhealthy. Warrington during the last 20 years had made great sanitary progress indeed. (Hear, hear.) It had been described as an extremely advanced town on sanitary matters. Councillor GREHNIIqG supported Councillor Robert's motion. _ _
Councillor Mom asked if there was a precedent for the Council disintegrating a committee ? He thought the motion was quite out of order. The Tow's CLERK declared the discussion in order.

Councillor It. T. FAIRCLOUGH suggested that the cleansing of the streets should be put in the hands of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. Courri!tor Puntrros supported the motion of Coun- cillor Roberts. He said that he had been informed that this subject had been brought forward at a meeting of the Sanitary Committee, but that the Chairman had over-ruled the question. He added that he brought to the notice of the Chairman the fact of a man who had succumbed to small-pux being removed to the mortuary on a Monday night, and left there till the succeeding Thursday, when the body was interred. The Chairman said that he did not know anything about it, but prom- ised to inquired into the subject. After investigation he told him privately that such a thing had occurred, but he had not been able to find who was responsible—the Sanitary Committee, the Cemetery Committee, or the Board of Guardians. He also informed the Council that he knew of cases where houses that had been infected had not been disinfected for almost a week._ .‘

Alderman Surrov : Is this not going too far . Councillor PLIMPTON replied that he wanted to show that the Sanitary Committeso had too much work to dp, and that matters were not being attended to as they ought to be. Alderman SurroN : We know that, we admit it.
Councillor PLUNTTON : Then it is for the Council to say that the Sanitary Committee has not been attending to its work, and that its labours should be divided.
Alderman SurToN : We all sav_so,

Councillor BIACKIIIIRST remarked that there was a great deal of force in what Councillor Roberts had said. There wac much work to be done on the committee, from which, however,he should have liked the resolution to have emanated. _ . .

CouncillorGßEEN suggested that the appointment of a committee to consider the whole mattgr. There was a great deal of overlapping in the work of committees, and the suggestion he had made would enable them to determine where it existed.

Councillor ErixON said the Lonvford Depot was in the worst condition of any sanitary depart of the five cor- porations which were making dry excreta. The MAYOR : Confine yourself to the motion. Councillor Drxow looked steadfastly at the Mayor apparently in surprise, but made no remark. The MAYOR : Won't you go on ? Councillor Drxow : I won't go on. The MAYOR : If you don't I shall call upon Alderman Harrison (who had risen to speak) to address the Coun- cil.

Councillor Drxmr still remained standing. Alderman HARRISON contended that an admirable case had been made out by Councillor Roberts, and no one could find fault with the moderation with which he had introduced his motion, hut it looked a little disrespectful to the Sanitary Committee to take the drastic course which had been suggested. The MAYOR (to Councillor Dixon) : Are you going to speak or not ? Councillor DIXON haying made one or two remarks resumed his seat.

Councillor Ropmrrs in replying, said the Council was responsible far the government of Warrington, and not any particular committee, and it was because he con- sidered it opportune that he had brought forward his motion that night. Alderman Chandley was usually correct, but he had misquoted that evening. fie had said that in the multitude of counsellors there was wisdom.

Alderman CIIANDLEY : I said 'plenitude." Councillor ROBERTS : I am not going to swagger about my knowledge of scripture. Alderman CHANDLEY I was not aware it was Scrip- ture. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS : The quotation is, " In the multi- tude of counsellors there is safety," and it is because I believe that even in a multitude of town councillors there is a maximum of safety that I appear to-night in support of my motion. The motion was then put and carried without dissent.
