HO 11 RT BLE MIIRD AND MUTILATION OF A WOMAN AT GLASGOW —A diabolical murder, somewhat resembling the noto- rious " Jack the Ripper " outrages, was committed in Glasgow en Tuesday morning. The scene of the murder was the fashionable district of Pollokshields, in the south-west of the city. At noon the police were informed that the body of a woman, horribly mutilated, had been discovered in the garden of West Lodge, occupied by the family of the late Mr. Wilson, who was for many years a leading member of the Corporation of Glasgow. The details of the tragedy are of the most shocking description, equalling anything in the annals of crime. The supposed murderer is a gardener named William M'Ewan, about 40 years of age, who was kept as a caretaker on the premises at West Lodge during the absence of the' family. He is a native of county Down, Ireland. He occupied a small room on the ground floor of West Lodge. He was seen on Monday night about six o'clock by a neighbouring gardener, and at that time all was apparently right. This man, named M'Dougall, who was in the habit of going into M'Ewan's room to cook his food, tapped at the window on Tuesday morning at six o'clock as usual. M`Ewan at once replied "Oh, all right. lam not going out this morning; lam sleepy." M'Dougall then left and went to his work. On returning at eight o'clock he went into the room, and at once observed that something was amiss, because of the confused condition of the con- tents of the place. He communicated with the police- man on the beat, and an inspection of the place disclosed the fact that a murder had been perpetrated. On the centre of the floor was a large pool of blood, while the two beds in the place were turned up, as were almost all the articles in the room. Blood was sprinkled all over the apartment, while the bedclothing and a quantity of wearing apparel lying about the floor were besmeared with blood. No trace of the gardener or of the body of the vistim being found, a search was made in the vicinity. Blood marks were found all over the courtyard, access to which was had from the apartment. Following the marks of blood the searchers observed what appeared to be four little mounds in the garden. On digging up one of these they found the head and right arm of a woman ; under the second they came upon the mutilated trunk ; the left arm was under the third mound ; and the removal of the fourth disclosed other portions of the body. The victim was apparently a middle-aged woman with a flattened nose. An axe found in the apartment in which the murder was com- mitted had evidently been recently washed. Following some blood marks the offlcers w-era led to a tool-house, where among the rubbish lying about they unearthed the half of a large saw that was clotted with blood, and from the appearance of this instrument there could be ' no doubt that the body had been sawn to pieces with it. There was also found an ordinary biscuit box I clotted with blood, in which, it is thought, M'Ean I took the body piece by piece and buried it in the garden.

M'Esvan has been known in the district for the last five years, but has been employed at West Lodge for less than a year. The body of the murdered woman is sup- posed to be that of Mary Anderson, wife of a painter. Mrs. Anderson, who had been living apart from tier hus- band,disappeared a few days ago. So tar as can be ascer- tained it is probable that the crime was committed at an early hour on Tuesday morning. The last perm be- sides the accused and his victim in the apartment is supposed to have been the neighbouring gardener M'Dougall, who left M'Ewan in the place at six o'clock on Monday night. CAPTURE AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF WEWAN.

M'Ewan, the man who was being sought by the police for his supposed complicity in the murder, was captured on Wednesday afternoon, under the following circum- stances. At five minutes to two, while three game- keepers of Sir John Stirling Maxwell were walking along the road between Glasgow and Paisley, their attention I was attracted by a man proceeding in a leisurely manner lon the other side of the hedge. The head gamekeeper, named Cox, thinking he was a poacher, asked what he was doing there, but the man gave no answer. Another of the keepers put the same question, whereupon the man pulled out a small pocket knife and began to cut his throat. The three gamekeepers jumped over the hedge with all speed, and prevented him doing himself further harm. The keepers then concluded 'that the man was the fugitive M'Ewan, and one of them accordingly ran for a policeman, and found one at a place called the Halfway House. The constable immediately came and identified M'Ewan as the man wanted. The fugitive was carried to a smithy, and a policeman, who was scouring the :country on a bicycle in search of M'Ewan, hurried to the nearest subsurban telephone station and telephoned to headquarters in Glasgow. An ambulance wagon from Govan was ulti- Mately obtained, and M'Ewan was conveyed to the Glasgow Royal Infirmary. He did not speak on the road, and when he arrived at the Infirmary he was greatly exhausted, and his face was ghastly pale. His neck had been bound up with a child's pinafore. On his being carried into the casualty ward Dr. Henderson found that M'Ewan had inflicted upon himself a diago- nal wound from the left ear to the middle of the throat, three inches long and one inch deep, but as the blood was coagulated it is impossible to say as yet whether the wound is dangerous or not. The doctor, however, expressed himself as hopeful that M'Ewan will recover. The news of the arrest spread rapidly, and a large crowd peered through the Infirmary railings to get a glimpse of the unhappy man as he was carried into the ward.

The murdered woman was identified during the after- noon as Lizzie O'Connor, an unfortunate. A man named M'Neilly, who was brought up on Wed- nesday in custody in connection with the revolting tragedy, is a sailor employed in the steamship Furnessia, which is just now lying in Glasgow harbour. He has stated that he and M'Ewaia met a woman in the street and persuaded her to accompany them to West Lodge. She went with M'Ewan into the room he occupied and remained there, as far as he (M'Neilly) knew, all night. He slept in another room of the house, but left early in the morning in time to reach his work at six o'clock. M'Neilly denies having seen the murder committed or taken any part in it.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 15. 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 15. 1892.
ACCIDENTS AT HAYDOCK COLLEMES.

James Shimmin, of Earlestoorn, a surface man at the Queen Pit, Haydock, has had a narrow escape from a terrible death. He was pushing some boxes to the pit shaft when he slipped, and would have fallen headlong to the bottom but for the providential fact that the cage was nearing the top, and it struck him on the face and forced him on to the bank again. As it was, he received an ugly wound, and now lies in the Cottage Hospital attended by Dr. Hayward.—Two other accidents are also reported. John *Valentine, of Parr, was working in the Haydock foundry yard, when a cage hoop,,which he was repairing, fell upon and severely crushed his foot.—Jam Colefield, of New Boston, Hay- dock, was also seriously injurel on the leg by a stone falling from the roof of the Harman ah Colliery.
A LIFE-BOAT SA TU RDAY FOR
WARRINGTON.
MEETING AT THE iOWN HALL.

With the object of establishing a " Life-boat Saturday 'lit—Warrington, the Mayor—convened a meeting of ladies, which was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Monday afternoon. The Mayoress (Mrs. Edward Greenall, jun.) pre- sided over a large attendance cf ladies.

The MAYOR explained the object of the meeting, and expressed a hope that the meeting would be a succe se. He hoped the ladies would take up the movement in a hearty manner. If they did so, it was sure to be a success.

The Maroaass spoke as follows :—We meet this after- noon to *insider the coestion of establishing in Warring- ton a "Lite-boat Saturslay." Ladies' committees in other places have been most successful, and we see no reason why we in Warrington should be behindhand in this matter. The Lifeboat Institution, we all know, is well worthy of support, and ought to receive it from inland manufacturing towns, which depend so largely on cargoes from abroad. The funds of the Institution are most inadequate. Last year its income was £69,000, £lOO,OOO being the amount required. In Lancashire and Yorkshire, Life-boat Saturday has been wonderfully successful. In 1890 the subscription from these counties was £3,000 ; last year the amount received was £21,000 ; and this differ- ence was due to the great impetus given by awakening interest in Life-boat Saturday: the opportunity is given to everyone to subscribe a coin, no matter how small. and by so doing enabling the life-boat men to be better paid, and in time we hope to provide funds sufficient to grant men incapacitated by the work, or widows and orphans left desolate, some pension, which at present the Institution is unable to do. Surely the life-boat men are in a humble way heroes. No matter how ter- , rifle the storm,no hesitation is ever seen in the manning I of the boat,and one gre it need of a larger income is that the newest and best contrived boats may be provided in place of many which are nearly useless. For these brave men we are trying to awaken interest in Warring- ton, and I ask you, one and all, to help us to make " Life-boat Saturday "in Warrington, a great success, and to do all in your power to interest people around you in this matter. In Manchester the Local Com- mittee have decided to make the Life-boat Saturday an annual affair, and on the first of this month a second I collection was made, but the amount realized has not I yet been published. The movement has become a most popular one, and many towns are this year inaugurat- ing a Life-boat Saturday, and there is every reason to hope that the Life-boat Saturday will become a per- manent institution, and he just as much recognised as Hospital Sunday. Oh the motion of Mrs. Pickmere, seconded by Mrs. Butterworth, it was resolved" That this meeting of the ladies of Warrington heartily approve of the proposal of the Mayor to establish a Life-boat Saturday in Warring- ton, and that a Ladies' Committee be appointed for the purpose of assisting in the movement." On the motion ef Mrs. Broadbent, seconded by Mrs. Edelsten, it was decided that the Mayoreas be appointed president of the Ladies' Council, and M'rs. Broadbent was elected vice president, and Mrs. A. Edelsten (Beld-st.),.hon. secre- tary. The following ladies were appointed an Executive Committee :'—The President, Vice-President; Mrs. Pick. mere, Mrs. Smethurst, Mrs. W. Tinsley, Mrs. Butter- worthrMrs..Kerry,.Nfrs..Vere Davies,. Mrs. Monks, and Mrs. H. Woods. It was decidesiron the metion.of Mrs. R. T. Fairclough; seconded by Min. Edleston . to suggest the sth. of November- as the'day upearvridoh, Life-boat Saturday shall be held: The following ladies- were appointed a' Central' Conneii for the purpose of raising funds in aid of the Royal National Life-boat Institution, with power to add to their number, namely : Lady Greenall, Mrs. Broadbent Mrs. Vere Davies, Miss Tinsley, Mrs. and Miss Smet- hurst, Mrs. Monks, Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. Venn, Mrs. A. div.head: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT MANCHESTER.
div.p: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT MANCHESTER.

On Saturday the sergeants of the Cheshire and Lancashire Infantry brigades, who were encamped together at Conway during the summet,inaugurated their annual dinner at the Manchester Limited Restaurant, Royal Exchaage. The event was a great success. About 250 sat down to dinner, the corps re- presented being Ist, 2nl, and 3rd Volunteer Battalions of the Lancashire Fusiliers from Bury, Rochdale, and Salford, respectively; the Ist and 2nd Volunteer Batta- lions South Lancashire Regiment, from Warrington and St. Helens; and the 3rd, 4th, and sth Volunteer Batta- lions Cheshire Regiment. The Mayor of Warrington had promised to accompany the Warrington contingent, but at the last moment found himself unable to do so. Amongst those present from Warrington, however, were Alderman Francomb, Captain Ridgway, Captain Hutch- inson, and the sergeants of the Battalion. Others pre- sent included the Mayor of Middleton,Colonel Howarth, of the 3rd V.B.L.F.,.the Rev. J. E. Gull, chaplain to the brigade, and many officers. The brigade staff were unable to attend, but sent letters expressing their best wishes for the success of the gathering. After dinner the evening was spent convivially, several toasts being honoured, including "Major-General Thackwell and the Brigade Staff," proposed by Bugle-Major Jutton, 3rd V.R.L.F., and the songs and instrumental selections were contributed in ample number and with every indica- tion of appreciation. The chair was occupied by Sergt.- Major Tyson, of the 2nd V.8.5.L., senior sergeant- major of the brigade. Alderman Francomb gave "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," and Captain Ridg- way also spoke. The arrangements were excellently carried out by a committee composed of sergeants from each battalien, with Sergeant W.T.Halsall; 3rd V.8.L.F.. as hon. secretary.

WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. The annual meeting of this Council was •held in the Cocoa Rooms, Horsemarket-st., on Tuesday evening, Mr. Wright presiding. The report and balance sheet were submitted. The former con- tamed the following paragraph :—"The Council cannot, as in previous years, show an increase in membership, but a decrease, consequent upon the branches of the unions they were affiliated with becom- ing defunct. That being the reverse of the object of the Council we are pleased to state that it has increased in number of societies." The report, referring to the demonstration on June 11th last, stated :—" An inci- dent happened in connection with the demonstration that was disappointing to the public, which was no fault of the Council, viz., that Mr. Tom Mann was to have figured as the principal speaker, but immediately after the procession he left Warrington for another engage- ment in Leicestershire, without having (prior to coming to Warrington) given the Council any intimation of such engagement." The repoit also contained the following —" Having briefly referred to the important questions of the Council, we urge the desiranility of those trades not yet connected with it to become so at once. There are still some notable societies w hich keep aloof from co-operation, and we trust the mem- bers of those trades will see the necessity of coming forward to examine for themselves the question of a complete federation, as such a federation was a struggle for the betterment of labour as a whele. The subject of Direct Labour Repesentation has for some time past engaged the attention of the Council, it having become apparent that if the workers of the country wish to improve their position and advance the interests of their class, it can be best accomplished by sending members of their own class to represent them, whether locally or imperially. We are aware of the fact that some of the societies who hold themselves aloof from the Council look upon it of late as a political institution. We would not for a moment wish it to be understood as such, or that discord should exist, and sincerely hope that all petty jealousies of that description will be put aside. On nearly every hand the same hostile spirit is evinced towards the just claims of the working classes throughout the country. In conclusion we cannot r j )ice in as prosperous a trade as in our last report. Which- way we look the outlook is not one to cause the feelings of the working-man to rise to anything like exultation. The balace sheet showed an income (including a balance of £1 2s. 3p, at the commencement of the year) of £64135. 4d., and an expenditure of £4B 103. 10d., the balance, 17s. 6d. having been remitted to the Bromsgrove nailmakers. The officers for the ensuing year were elected as follows :—President, Mr. Wright, filesmiths' society ; vice-president, Mr. Malkin, ironworkers' society ; trea- surer, Mr. Waring; secretary, Mr. W. Bullock.

div.head: DISASTROUS COLLISION AT SEA.
div.p: DISASTROUS COLLISION AT SEA.

FOUR PASSENGERS CRUSHED TO DEATH. NEW YORK, MONDAY.—News has reached New York of a disastrous collision in the neighbourhood of Port Town- send, Massachusetts, which occurred on Saturday after- noon, between the collier Williamet and the Canadian Pacific Company's steamer Premier. The force of the collision was so great that the cabin of the Premier wa4 penetrated and four of the passengers were almost instantly crushed to death. One individual, terror - struck by the catastrophe, leaped into the sea and drowned, while at 'east twenty others received injuries. Both vessels were damaged to such an extent that it was necessary to beach them without delay.

div.head: I WRECK AT BLACKPOOL.
div.p: I WRECK AT BLACKPOOL.
GREAT DAMAGE TO THE NORTH PIER.

A scene of unparalleled excitement took place at Black- pool on Sunday morning. The wind rose on Saturday evening, accompanied by froquent heavy showers of blinding rain.- it-blesr-vaas• hard--eltarine- the night. When morning broke the gale had by no means abated. and as the day progressed the violence of- the hurricane seemed to increase rather than diminish. The sea was very rough, and the waves ran exceedingly high. A strict watch was kept seaward by the local boatmen, and between ten and eleven in the morning a three-masted vessel Was observed some distance out at sea obviously labouring heavily. The movements of the vessel were watched with the greatest apprehension, and ultimately it was seen that the worst tears concerning the boat were about to be realised. By noon it was fully evident that the crew had lost all command of their vessel, and that she was steadily coming nearer shore. The news of the impending disaster quickly spread, and despite the fact that the waves were washing continuously over the promenade, accompanied by drenching spray, every sheltered corner was occupied by spectators, eagerly watching the onward course of the doomed craft. At first it seemed as though the vossel would come ashore almost exactly between the two piers. Had that been the case the whole crew would most certainly have been drowned. Those on board realised that certain death awaited them if they drove on the hulking, and it was consequently a relief to the anxious watchers when the vessel was steered towards the North Pier. Several hundred persons were watching the pro- gress of events from the pier, and about one o'clock, when the ship was seen coming towards the structure with an ever-increasing momentum, there was a general rush to get off the pier before the craft struck it. Get- ting within the broken water inshore, on came the barque with awful swiftness, and as the was now within 50 yards of the hulking, and only a few yar Ss from the pier, the spectators held their breath as they anticipated the awful consequences. The vessel, however, struck the pier with a glancing movement, and for a moment rebounded with the shock. Had she caught the struc- ture lysw first she would most assuredly have crashed straight through it and imperilled the lives of many who were still on the pier, in addition to those of the unfor- -1 tunate crew. The deck of the vessel was about on a level with the pier, and immediately she struck it there ensued a scene of intense excitement. The crew were clustered at the stern, and one by one they jumped or were pulled from the aressel on to the pier by the life- boat men and others who had assembled to render assistance. Crash came the ship against the pier, and one of the sailors would be landed. She would then fall away for a few moments, hut the next wave would again send her against the pier, and more of the crew would be rescued. All this time the rescuers themselves were in the greatest danger. The pier had stood the buffeting remarkably well, but all at once, just when the last man was hanging suspended over the side, crash came the barque again, and a good por- tion of the pier, within a few feet of where the rescuers had been standing, was carried away and fell into the boiling surf. By this time, however, the crew of ten men and a boy had all been pulled on to the pier, and there was a general rush for the promenade when the vessel drifted inshore and broke down nearly the whole of the sloped entrance to the pier. The four shops built on the south side of the slope were all carried completely away. The shops, respectively, were used for the sale of sweets, furs, fancy goods and mechanical washers, and their valuable contents were entirely lost. The vessel drove broadside against the hulking within 20 yards of the promenade itself, and, as its bow had become wedged in the dismantled pier entrance it con- tinued to dislodge the supporting columns and twist the girders. Every wave broke over the vessel, the rigging was quickly washed away and in less thee half an hour from the moment she first struck the pier, the three mutt had fallen overboard,one on the promenade itself, and one on the pier, smashing the entrance gates. The vessel was a total wreck. As they cause off the pier the rescued crew and the hand of rescuers were enthusiastically cheered. The ship- wrecked sailoss were at once put into cabs and driven to the Wellington Hotel, where they were supplied with hot drinks and a good meal by Alderman Bickerstaffe, who all through took a leading part in the work of the rescue. The delight of the men at being saved from what seemed to them certain death was undoubted. The captain in his excitement danced about on the pier and waved his cap. The vessel turned out to be the Sirene, of 687 tonnage, owned by the Norwegian firm of Olsen and Tjome, Norway. The captain's name is Anders A. Gjutsen, and the crew of eleven are all Norwegians. The captain states that the vessel was towed out of the port of Fleetwood at noon on Saturday, bound in ballast for a port in Florida, North America, where they in- tended to load with timber. He had not got faraway when the vessel became unmanagable in the gale of Sunday morning, and she gradually drove ashore. The captain says he recognised that the only chance of sav- ing the lives of the crew was to start for the South side of the pier, and this he did, with the consequence already stated. It is roughly estimated that the damage done to the North Pier will amount to not less than £5,000. In addition to almost the whole of the entrance being carried away, the structure is badly damaged for more than half its length. The promenad- ing deck has been partly carried away, the supporting columns displaced, and the girders bent. The contents of the shops which were washed away by the sea repre- sent several hundred pounds. The managers and the !mail directors of the pier were early on the scene, but they were powerless to prevent the destruction Within an hour of the Sirens striking the pier the whole prom- enade was littered from end to end with debris. The wreck of the Sirens at Blackpool caused no further damage to the North Pier on Monday. The vessel herself received great damage from the high tide on Sunday night and will no doubt be broken-up as she lies.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
CADISHEAD.

The continuual downpour of rain has caused mach inconvenience to the dredging operations in the.neigh- bourhood. The barrier across No. 2 cutting. was care- fully watched on Sunday. In anticipation of a possible breakage, the dredger Rollin was moored near theriver, and steam was got up. By Monday the water in the cutting had risen to such a height that the engineers were enabled to steam into the river, and the dredger wag moored out of osnger in Na. 1 cutting. Here it is proposed to commence dredging in co-operathri with the dredger Glazeturook and the grads.

INQUEST AT LATCHFORD. Mr: Yates, coroner ,f the,district, held an inquest at the Latchford hospital, on Monday, on the body of Robert Nicholas (351, a native of Windham, near Nor- wich. who died from the effects of injuries received on the 24th ult. On the day in question the deceased was seen on Warrington Bridge, en his way to the huts at Acton Grange, where he lived, and on the following toorning he was found lying on his back at the bottom of a cutting intc which he had evidently fallen. He had to lie all night in the cutting with his hack and some ribs broken. Ishmael Ball, living in Norton, said the deceased was his cousin, and was a natiyeof Windham, near Norwich. He saw the deceased in the hospital, and he (deceased) told him he had missed his road. Doctor Walker said he was present when the deceased was admitted to the hospital. Deceased was suffering from injuries to the back, broken ribs, and lacerated lungs. He was also suffering from the effects of drink. He died from paralysis, the result of the injuries. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: CYCLISTS AND IIOAD OBSTRUCTIONS
div.p: CYCLISTS AND IIOAD OBSTRUCTIONS

Before Judge Shand, at the County Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Reid, journalist, of Bolton, sued Thomas Ball, contrre-or, Park-road. St.Fielens, for personal injuries received by him and damages to his bicycle by reason of the defendant's negligence at Huyton, on the 3rd July. Mr. Mackay (Messrs. Mackay and Cornish, Liverpool) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. P. Mearns (St. Helens) defended. It was stated that early on the morning of the day named the plaintiff and a companion started on their machines to make a journey from Liverpool to Newcastle. When near the Blue Bell Inn, Huyton, plaintiff, who was riding on the right side of the road, ran into a wagon which Was placed horizontally across the road. The night was very dark, and there was neither light on the wagon or anyone in charge to warn ypople of their danger. Reid's machine was damaged, while he was injured about the head, besidea receiving a severe shock to the system The two men returned to Liverpool, and plaintiff was afterwards attended by Dr. M`Cann, of Liverpool. For the defence it was explained that the wagon suddenly broke down an the road, and the driver left the wagon in order to obtain assistance for its repair or removal. He, however, engaged a man to look after the wagon during his absence, but the man disappeared, and neg. lected his duty.—His Honour remarked that Mr. Mearns had failed to prove contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff, and gave judgment for the plaintiff for £l4 4s. and costs (including LIO for personal in)uriesi, £3 3s. for doctor's fee, and one guinea for the damage to the machine.

OVER thirty years ago, TENNYSON The ' in" Locksley Hall" sang "of the New Era. brotherhood of man, the federation of the world-;" and before his time Burns gave expression to similar ideas. We are a long way as yet from the realisation of these views—dreams some people call them— but there can be no ques- tion that prefient-day thought runs more and more in the direction of brotherhood. It is the basis of ranch of the Socialism that is promulgated, and it underlies and stimulates the agitation in the , labour world. The Churches, too, are taking the matter up, and there is one organ which is devoted to chronicling and reviewing the work of the vari- ous religious bodies in this connection. Its title is "The New Era." It is issued monthly, price two- pence; it is admirably edited, and numbers amongst its occasional contributors eminent pro- fessors in this and other countries, besides giving the opinions of the clergy, and the leaders of the working-classes. As might be expected, there is some confusion of tongues. While there is agree- ment upon the ends to be achieved, there is much diversity of opinion us to the methods to be pur- sued. For instance, Mr. J. H. WlLsorr, M.P., who has been addressing the chemical workers of St. Hehms, sees no necessity as yet for the working- claxses setting .up a separate party in politics. Mr. IiEIR HARDIE, on the other hand, urges that ' "the labour party must be above suspicion of be- ing connected with any other party." The time may come when that advice can with advantage be carried out, but that time is not yet. It was seen, at the General Election at Newcastle, that action upon these lines meant playing into the hands of the Tory party; and, by detaching Liberal votes, it meant, too, robbing the Liberals of a seat. Happily the working-classes profited by the mis- take ;so that when Mr. Joint MORLEY sought re-

election they rallied round him, and his return was a triumph of the most totable kind. -, "The New Era," whilst fostering as it Zees every movement which has for its object the bet- terment of the masses, renders • a great service in placing before its readers the views of trained men who give calm but earnest thought to the problems. of the day. Its records are necessarily at times. records of failures, but it is this way that men are enabled to "rise from stepping-stones of their dead selves to higher things." Toe experiments of Lord BIELASSEY are a case in point. They have failed,. and yet he is deserving of every credit for having: made the experiments. Anxious to relieve the poor in the congested districts of London,. he purchased land in Western Australia and. in Canada with a view to colonising. He'. sent out selected fawilies—some three hun- dred persons altogether—the project requir- ing that they &mild begin as labourers, and rise gradually to the condition of indepea- dent farmers. " Having," we are told" paid their passage and settled the emigrants on the land, he shared the general experience in similar cases, for. in a few weeks the greater:number of those who had been sent out to Canada had left their eni- ployment: The labourers look on the repayment, of advances as an irksome obligation, and Lord BRASSICY has been forced to the conviction that colonisation cannel: be conducted on business principles." Such a result must be iliscouraging to Lord BRASSEY ; but it may have been that there were special causes for the failure. The Cockney is essentially social and gregarious ; and it is not unlikely that the quietude of farm life in Canada, after the bustle oi London, would be dis- tressing in its monotony. In any case, the experie ment is not one to be repeated under similar conditions ; and that is something learned. Why not seek to find Englishmen Work on English land? Why not try to relieve the congestion of our large centres of population by giving fain' labourers who now make to towns sufficient iu- ducement to stay in the country? To aeeure" plish this, we require a radical reform of our land laws. There must be an abolition of the mischievous customs and enactments relating to entail and primogeniture: the pewer of " the dead hand " must be checked. The laud must be sei free ; the acquirement of allotments meds easY; and villegers, like townsmen,. must be given con- trol. of their .own affairs. In short, the 110SV era niuse be one of equality of opportunity, and of a fairer division of the fruits of industry.

AN Torrington has frequently called of attention to the insanitary f the houses in the courts condition and alleys the neighbourhood of Dial-street, Fennel-street, and in Cockhedge-lane ; and some time ago we included this district in a series of articles, on the Black. In January last, the Sanitarl Committee, recognising the fact that, under the Public Health Acts, the matter might be brought before the Local Government Board, instructed the Medical Officer of Health and the Bor°4ll Surveyor to prepare a special report on this,ins- tary area. That report was prepared and printed so far back as April 26; but for some reason or another, which we have been unable to fathom, it has never been dealt with by the Sanitary Committee, or even submitted to the Town Council. The other week the Rev. John Yonge, one of the few ministers in Warrington who recognise that the people have bodies as well as souls to be saved, made in- quiry as to the report through the medium of our columns ; but be could obtain no informa- tion. The apology has been made that, with an epidemic of scarlet fever and smallpox to grapPle with, it was impossible to deal with the report; but that apology only covers part of the case; for it ought to be kuown that the report was Pre- pared three months before the outbreak of firma' , pox! Why, we would ask—and the ratepayers ought to insist upon an answer—has the reP°lt been kept back all these months; and, further, why is it still being kept hack? Is it doe to the action or inaction of Alderman BURGESS that it has not been made public? Under circumstances, it was a stroke of luck for the "easel to bo thrown as it was against the pier; but 15therw'Ise it would not only have been wrecked, the crew would have been drowned with tla,°llsands looking on, though unable to render aftistance. -- 4,eari the King of Italy have'been pondering on 44• 3speare's lines which run— AO, let the candied tongue lick absurd pomp, • crook the pregnant hinges of the knee 1, here thrift may follow fawning? :,11-4 certainly does not desire to be fawned upon in ;nu:Latter of gifts and subscriptions for his silver '4ding ; and has written a letter to that effect. 04 concluding he says :—" I pray you, Mr. Presi- tO make this firm determination known to th Public representatives and to the citizens, so any idea of such subscriptions may be dis- COW, or, if already carried- into execution, that 0.7: sums collected may be turned to works of !_itlr." -- ,Couneillor Smethurst, of Warrington, has no a'aat sympathy with Free Education. At a meet- the Town Council, on Tuesday, he urged ulat free places should not be provided, unless 0' had sufficient proof that free schooling was icar What is "sufficient proof," and who T• 0 determine the proof? As Councillor Shaw- Put it, parents have a right to demand • places for their children ; and it is the duty of al: local authority to do all they can in a legitim- -00 Way to see that this right is not ignored. uracillo eth_ r Smethurst is no doubt like many an- ther Tory in wishir.g his party had not played education card, 'seeing that they have not either a "trick " or " honours by it. r 441 r that the Warrington Town Council has ed by a large majority that it is desirable at the • "Itaitt present heavy duties of the Sanitary 4 It ia ee should devolve upon two committees, t t, a matter of course to say that steps will be when the new committees are formed next

month, to givo the resolution practical effect. Councillor Pll,ll,oberts, who moved the resolution, fully made out his case. Indeed, it is not too much to say that it has been obvious flr years to ineinhprs of the Council, and to. many i•itepayirs, that duch a reform was not only desiral;le but absolutely necessary.

The resolution may be said to have been carried without opposition, though Councillor .Muir, like a good old-fashioned Tory, seemed afraid that becauee it was proposed_ to do something now. must be something wrong ? He twice asked the question whether there was a "'precedent for the Council to disintegrate a Committee ?" No answer was given, for nobody was quite sure whether Councillor Muir knew himself what he was driving at? Can it be that he has heard so much from Tory jplatforms about "disintegration of the empire ' that be has gut "disintegration" on the brain f

It knay be nows to Crinncillor Muir to be informed that what Councillor Roberts prop,ses is not " to disintegrate a committee." . " To. disin- egrate" is to break up a solid into its integrant particles ; but Councillor! Roberts proposes the formation of two solid bodies—that is two com- mittees instead of One. However, using the "Wor'd " disintegrate " properly, there is a plain answer to Councillor,Muir's question ; for there is such a thing "as a precedent for the Council to disin- tegrate a•committee." As a matter of fact every committee is disintegrated every year, when it is dissolved by effluxion of time; each committee is broken up, that is to say, into integrant particles. In this way, Councillor Muir will becoine.a par- ticle at the end of this mentli—a pirticle which may disappear on the let of November.

SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN COURSER.

At the recent coursing meeting of the Ridgway Club, Lytham, Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., of Runcorn, had several dugs competing, and they were highly successful. A sporting contemporary thus refers to the event : "Everyone was pleased to see an old supporter of coursing in Mr. J. Brundrit have a turn at last, and not only win a few courses but divide one of the principal stakes. The Runcorn courser scarcely raised a flag last year or the _year before, and his dogs had come to be a sort of bye-word and reproach. The surprise was, therefore, all the greater. His representatives, on Wednesday and Thursday, with long odds against them, won course after course, and when Bessie Oliver got to the end of the South Lancashire Stakes the owner came in for no end of congratulations. Mr. Brundrit's new trainers Adamson, was some twenty years with Sir Thomas Brocklebank, and William is entitled to great credit for the wonderful improvement he has made in the dogs that have been placed under his charge."

At Nantwich, Mr. Roger 0. Richards, assistant commissioner in connection with the Royal Corai mission on Labour, has held an inquiry into the conditions of agricultural labourers in Cheshire. It was stated that the supply of labourers was not sufficient for farmers. During the past ten or fif- teen years the supply had decreased, the labourers having migrated to the industrial centres. Some of the farmers who were present at the inquiry sug- gested that more cottages should be provided, and that land should be attached to them wherever practicable ; also that teachings in agricultural sub- jects should be given in rural schools and that the County Council should encourage this by offer- ing prizes. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.— Ade. THE WEST LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE. From inquiries made on Tuesday regarding the condition of the various trades in St. Helens and throughout this portion of West Lancashire, there can be no doubt that trade generally is in a de- pressed state, and the outlook for the winter is not a very favourable one. This condition of affairs is affecting the coal trade, and prices are said to be failing. Strangers find difficulty in getting em- ployment, but wages remain as previously. With regard to the Haydock coalfield, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., the St. Helens Collieries Company, and other district firms, trade is pretty busy, and work is going on five days per week. The reason for this apparently settled con- dition of things is practically owing to the coal- fields name.d being in close proximity to the best markets for fuel. -

div.head: fiURIAL HITCH AT WARGRAVR CHURCH.
div.p: fiURIAL HITCH AT WARGRAVR CHURCH.

On Tuesday afternoon an unpleasant hitch, caus- ing much inconvenience to the patties conct-rned occurred in respect to the burial of the body of an old man named Jatnes Vaudrey. .The funeral was arranged to take place at three o'clock, and a family grave had been opened in preparation for the body. Just at the last moment, however, the rector, Rev. J. Uarson, objected to the coffin being put into the grave, on the ground that it would be too near the surface of the earth, and stipulated that it should not be less than two feet. The sexton was sent off in hot haste to inform the parties, some of whom drove to the church yard in a atourniag coach. On arrival there, the rector still declined to allow the coffin to be placed in the grave, and no other course was left but to open a new grave. This was at once proceeded with, but it was not until nearly six o'clock that it was finished, at which time the interment took place.

Mr. Willis believed that he could solve the discol- ouration problem, and it was agreed that he should, with a jury of six to decide as to the merits of his work, give examples of his skill at three farms. The report on the proceedings Was submitted to the Council of the Chamber on Monday at Crewe. While unanimously of opinion that Mr. Willis's task had not been performed with complete success, the jury were convinced that much benefit had resulted in each case from his work. This opinion was sup- ported by the occupants of the farms visited, and Mr. Tollemache, M.P., who presided at the meeting said he believed that Mr. Willis was on the highroad to success in dealing with discolouration in cheese:

div.head: " SCRITTATOR."
div.p: " SCRITTATOR."

Who is it that delights to see, His foolish thoughts on paper? Who courage lacks, and signs himself Scrutator? Who poses as the poor man's friend ; Stands forth as a debater; Who never proves one half he says? Scrutator. Who would the poor deny of that, Which is essential, Wa-ter; Who bullies Heywood, Brandreth, too? Scrutator. Who tries to run our Guardians down? We think them two first-raters, And better far than twenty such— Scrutators. Who is it wants a Local Board ; Who wants to be Dictator, And vote for Guardians year by year? Scrutator.

Who badgers ex-offieios, Of whom hes ,6ucli a hater ? They go their way and never mind— Scrutator. Who is this man who hides his name, And signs himself " Serutator ?" A simpler one would do as well— " Pertater."

div.head: I CORPORATION oFWARRINGTON
div.p: THE I CORPORATION oFWARRINGTON
• AND THE SEXTON OF ST. PAUL'S.
A " GRAVE" QUESTION.
To the Editor of the "Examiner." 23, Winwick-street, Warrington Oct. 14th. 1892.
Dear Sir,— ST. rauL'a sErroN AND TRH CORPORATION.

The enclosed correspondence may interest some of your readers in connection with the recent discussion in the Town Council. Your readers should know that the fee received by the sexton, is is. for burials in one part of the Cemetery, and 4s. in other parts ; and that the swami's duties comprise other things besides digging and filling the graves. The Corporation them- selves do the grave digging and filling, and charge for it, and it is not to be supposed that in fixing the sexten's fee of is., the digging and filling up the graves were to be done by the sexton for that fee. It appears t me that the Corporation or certain of the members thereof, are lying down in what my old partner, Mr. J. F. Marsh, once termed" an equine:nidificatina," but which for the understanding of your non-classical readers. I will put in the vernacular a mare's nest," but which would perhaps in this case, be mere appropriat..ly termed, the nest of the humbler quadruped usually attached to a coster's vehicle. Yours truly, ' W. D. JEANti

[coin.] J. L. Whittle, Esq. 25, Win wick-st., Warrington, 3rd Oct., 1892. Dear Sir,— , ST. PAUL'S SEXTON'. We have been consulted by Mr. George Bebbington, the newly-appointed sexton, in reference to his position. We understand that the Corporation require him to per- form the duties of his office at the Cemetery. Will you be good enough to define what is meant ? Do the Col., poration require him to dig the graves and find all labour, Lie. ? We observe that in the list of burial fees is included Is. for sexton's fee in one ground, and 4.5. in other parts. Do you mean to contend that the sexton is required to dig a grave and fill it up for that fee? If so, we venture to say that your contention cannot be maintained. . The fee is evidently a merely nominal fee, which the sexton is entitled to by law. If the Corpora- tion really mean to require the sexton to perform the grave-digging, &c., then, of course, he will have to be paid for doing so. We can hardly imagine, however, that the Corporation mean to let the grave-digging and care of the Cemetery out of their own control. The assertion that the late sexton received the fees and did nothing for it, is entirely groundless and gratui- tous.

The sexton's and clerk's rights are reserved by law, and the Corporation cannot alter them. The Corpora- tion, of course, charge for digging the graves, &c., and they also charge the sexton's and clerk's fees, which they will be bound to band over to him otherwise they will hear further of it. We imagine the Cemetery Commit- tee must be in a bit of a fog, and they had better re- consider the position, and you will please let us know whether our client is to dig the graves or not. _ .
Yours truly, D. JEANS AND CO.
[cop.] Town Clerk's 01fices, Warrington, October 13:.13, 1892.
Dear Sirs,—

ST. PAUL'S SEXTON. I have received your letter of the 3rd instant, and in reply thereto all I have to say is th a the Corporation require the sexton of St. t'aul's t.) perform the duties of his office at the Cemetery. I may point out that up to the present the Corporation have not received any formal notice from the Vicar, of his appointment of your client as Sextiv of St. Paul's. Yours truly, J. LYON WHITTLE. Messrs. W. D. Jeans and Co., Solicitors.

25, Winwick-st., Warrington, 14th, 0;:t., 1892. Dear Sir,— We shall advise Mr. Bebbington that he is entitled to perform all the duties of sexton and to receive all fees for the duties. Will you be good enough to send us a list of the charges which tlse Corporation have hitherto made for doing the grave-s-liggintr, &c., arid state when Mr. Beb- bington may begin to do the work. ilave you a Ty of the order under which the charges and fees were fixed? And will you furnish us with a copy. Of course the taking over of the duties hitherto per- formed by the Corporation, will involve a radical change at the cemetery. However, as it is the Corporation's own will, let it he so.
Yours truly, W. D. JitsNs AND CO.

J. L. Whittle, Esq. - P.S.—You will of course understand that t will not necessarily follow that Mr. Behbinston will dig the graves himself, but that he will employ workmen to do the work as his deputies-S(T Burial Board of 11.,chester v. Thompson 6 L.R. C.P. 448. The Corporat it.)ll have hitherto done the grave-digging a:s deputies, and re- ceived the fees for it. W. D. JHANS AND CO.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEIIIO
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEIIIO
AT WAR RINGTON.

The number of smallpox cases still continues to increase though, fortunately, not so rapidly as a while ago. There have now been a total of 172 cases, 11 of these having occurred since ednes- day. A hope is entertained that the approach of cold weather will help to stamp out the disease. A report has been largely circulated in the town that Mr. Burrows, of Legh-st., who Is in the, .-,rnallpox Hospital had died of the disease, but this was Tilt true, as last night be was doing well. It has, we may mention been deemed necessary in consequ- ence of the epidemic to make restrictions as to the admission of visitors to the Infirmary. HOW VIE DISEASE IS SPREAD.

One of the difficulties which the authorities have to encounter is the utter carelessness or thought- lessness of a number of people, when signs of smallpox have made their appearance, and the necessity arises of removal to the hospital. In one case, we believe, the medical officer a health dis- covered that quite a little crowd of women had been visiting a patient, and that they had made off into another room on hearing of his approach. In other cases relatives had taken an affectionate part- log and kissed the patient when being removed to the hospital. Children had been brought from school to take leave of their parents, before they were taken away, ard one instance is mentioned in , which some scores of people gathered round an ! ambulance in order to witness the departure of a person to the hospital. In addition to this the officials had considerable difficulty in keeping people away from the hospital, and it is said that , one person resorted, in spite of all regulations, to various expedients in order to communicate directly or indirectly with those who were inside the hospital.

div.head: ACOMODATIuN FOR MORE PATIENTS.
div.p: ACOMODATIuN FOR MORE PATIENTS.

The Sanitary Committee have purchased from the authorities of the Girls' High School at Blackburn, for £l2O, three iron buildings and one wooden building, which will be put up on the ground adjoining the Hope Hospital. The iron buildings will be used as additional accomodation for patients, and are respectively of the dimensions of 56 feet in length by 26 feet in breadth, 29 feet by 6 inches, and 22 feet by 18 inches. The wooden building will be used for sleeping accomodation for the nurses, who at present have to sleep at the Aikin-st. Hospital. The buildings will be fixed up in the course of next week, an extra cost of course being incurred on this account. CORONER'S JURIES AND THE SMALLPDX.

At an inquest yesterday. as to the death by accident of a woman named Palfreman of Bostock-street, Inspec- tor Spihks said there was a great deal of smallpox in that neighbourhood. Mr. F. A. Jones, the deputy- coroner, who was conducting the inquest said that fact was another strong argument why the viewing of bodies was not always desirable. If he had known the district was infectmi he would not have called upon the jury to view the body.

div.p: OUTBREAK IN LIVERPOOL

The Medical Officer Tor L-iv—e—rp.ool reported to the Health Committee, on Thursday, sereral cases of smallpox in St. Anne-st., one in Ad , and one in the Newsboy's Home, Everton-road, aril one in Queen Anna-st. The Medical Officer stated that so far as he could gather the outbreak had been imported from War- rington through someone who stayed in a lod..!ing-trll3e in St. Anne-it. The total deaths for the week endiny, Saturday last were twenty-five below the a vera2es of the last ten years, and at the rate cf 21.9 per 1,000 of the estimated population.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORIMPONIMINT.
That there is no new development in connection with the Widnes Shoot Board electiou, but the candidates and their supporters are bard at work canvassing.
That in regall to the municipal election, the Liberal party are leaving no stone unturned to return their candidates, and there is no doubt that every effort will be needed to succeed.

That Mr. Shores has done a grand stroke for his party in having about 500 Conservatives struck off the Burgess List in consequence of objections raised by him, the Tory party not baying taken the trouble to'revise the list.
That the Conservatives have held a meeting but could not decide upon any come of action. and the election arrangements are left in the hands of Messrs. R. Lewis and James White.
That the Nationalists have not yet made a definite selection of their candidates.
That delays are dangerous in electioneering matters, and they should be up and doing if they mean to secure seats in the Council Chamber.
That the list of independents has increased by the addition of the names of Mr. .T. Bullough, and Mr. F. Neil. The other independents are Messrs. D. Wright, B. Brown, F. Heyes, and W. Christie.
That there is every prospect of a capital struggle between the numerous candidates.

That the outbreak of smallpox at Antrobus will not be altogether evil, if it causes the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority to build an infectious diseases hospital, because there is no means what- ever for dealing with an outbreak of disease.
That the quest ion of cost is secondary to the question of necesbity, and if a suitable institution could be erected for the sum mentioned by Dr. Adams, it Would be money well spent.

That it is satisfactory to know that while the Board of Commissioners are affecting to ignore Dr. lefJenilan's impeachment of the management of the llo,pital at Higner Runcorn, they have appointed a CommittOe to inquire into the condition and arrangements of the building, and the name of its administration.

That the attitude of Mr. Pritchard in regard to the Technical Institute will come as a surprise to many ; because it is generally supposed that the necessity for such an educational institution bad been proved, and that the provision of funds had almost passed the problematical stage.

That the Board School is altogether unsuited as at present arranged for the teaching of Science and Art, and as to erecting the Technical Institute on the land adjoining that building, the school is, at present overcrowded, and the School Board have , had a very strong hint from H.M. Irtepector that more accommodation must be provided, and they will, theref6re want the land themselves for a new school or an extension of the present one.

That unless the Commissioners bestir themselves in this work, the Runcorn Institute will not be built for years after a similar institution is put up at Widnes. Is there not as much public spirit in Runcorn as Widnes, and is Runcorn to be always in the rear in the educational race?

OPENING OF A WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL AT

HELSBY. On Friday afternoon week the new Wesleyan Sunday School at Helsby, was opened, when a sermon was preached hy the Rev. Char lea Garrett, of Liverpool, to a good congregation. Tbe rev, gentleman based his dis- course on Psalm cxviii, 29, •• 0 give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good : for His mercy endureth for ever." At the conclusion of this service tea, which was served by the ladies of the congregation, was partaken of by a goodly company. Subsequently a meeting was held in the chapel, under the presidency of Mr. J. R. Frith, of Runcorn, who was supported by the Rev. P. Pizey, the Rev. C. Garrett, and Mr. E. J. Guest. After devotional exercises had been indulged in, Mr. Guest submitted a financial statement, showing that £350 was required to pay for the work undertaken, Of this they had received in cash and proo4lseB £263, leaving a balance of £9O still to be obtained. He promised to give one-fourth of the amount that !night be raised at the opening srvices. The Chairman urged upon Wesleyans the great need there was for engaging in Sunday School work, and thus teaching the young s,,tind Christian principles. The Rev, Charles Garrett ref,Tred to the work in which lie was engaged amen!: po. II children in LiverpooLand gave a number of interestin in-,tances showing thegreat good that had already been accomplished. Other addresses were delivered, and ,co:lections were made on behalf of the school building Lind.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT GREAT SANKEY.

On Mond-a-i-a-n7i.c-cia;ni-;;;;;TeT;--MC:. William Taylor, of Brow Farm, Great Sankey. Mr. Taylor was ascending a ladder, when it suddenly slipped out at the bottom, causing him to fall heavily to the ground, breaking hit lea. Medical aid was at once summoned. the injured limb was se, and he is now progressing favourably. " INA Fix." _ .

On Saturday a curious.accident befel one of Mr. .I. R. Whalley's traction engines. The engine was about to begin the work of thrashing, at Mr. Lee's farm, Doe Green, but in taking up its position, the ground, softened by the recent rains, gave way and the two side wheels of the engine sank to the depth of about four feet and became firmly embedded. The men tried in vain to extricate it. On Sunday, Mr. Whalley with another engine and some work- men after a bard struggle managed to get the engine out of the bole. PENEETIT BAND OF HOPE.

The other evening a meeting Was held in the weOeyan Schools, Penketh, Mr. Robert Garnett in the chair, under the auspices of the Band of Hope connected with the Schools, When Mr. Whitehead, of Manchester, the well-known temperance lecturer, paid a visit on his refilin home after a successful tour through the United States. Mr. Whitehead chose for his subject, "Love, courtship, and marri- age." The lecture was full of humour, interspersed with numerous and appropriate temperance songs. There,was a good attendance, and the proceeds will be devoted to the temperance cause.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

I hear that the committee for making arrange- ments for the bazaar in aid of the funds of the Warrington Gymnasium, have deemeti it advisable to postpone for a short time, the nolding of the bazaar which was to have been opened during the present month. They have been advised to take this course in view of the prevailing sickness in the town. It is almost certain that if the bazaar were held at the present time it would suffer in conse- quence of the prevalent epidemic. The committee are put to same inconvenience by this delay, but I trust they will not suffer by it. Indeed, they ought to profit by it, as it will give the worliJrs an oppor- tunity of putting in a few "extras."

'Tie Liverpool Journal of Commerce" likes, I have often noticed, to have a rap at the Ship Canal. Tins is what is said in the current issue, and I give it beceuse Warrington is one af the municipalities referred to :—" The privilege of assisting this undertaking will, we hear, be sought by some other municipalities besides Manchester, and possibly by other public bodies. It will be remembered that Parliament refused its consent to the money of Salford ratepayers being so appropriated, though the ratepayers themselves were apparently anxious that it Should be. Mr. Marshall Stevens is to give his valuable ideas as to future traffic to a meeting lon Monday week. His figures will be • official,' and therefore, to Manchester shareholders and rate- payers. floubtless, conclusive. • Other people will judge them by otber standards."

What about the presentation to the Siayor in oinnection with the opening of the band stand? I see that the sum of £l4 of what,l suppose,is Corpor- tien money—for I hear of no subscription—has been applied to the purchase of a " solid silver inkstand unclosed in a handsome case" as a memento of that occasion and of his Worship's year of office.. Is not . this a new departure? I know it is usual to present a trowel in the case of the laying of a foundation stone, and a good deal has been said about the tiowel that was presented to Alderman Francomb, when Mayor, through lay- ing the foundation stone of the baths before the loan for the scheme had been sectioned by the Local Government Board. But, an inkstand I Clow does that come in, in connection with the opening of a band stand?

I do not wish to suggest that the Mayor is not SEI well entitled to a present. as any of his predeces- sors, but the question I wish to raise is, where are we to stop if presents are to be made on the occa- sion of every little ceremony? Even if it be said that. that is not intended, still, if the present chief magistrate has something given him as a memento of his year of office, the next chief magistrate will perhaps consider himself slighted if something equally as good be not given to him. For my part, I think it is a very questionable precedent to estab- lish. There can be no objection, of course, to the members of the Cerporation being generous if they will be generous at their own expense?

I am glad to see that there is to be a memorial of the late Mr. W. Sharpe, for there can be no question that he was a most estimable gentleman. But as I am this week in a critical mood, I would suggest that something better might be done with the Cl2O which it is proposed should be raised, than expend- ing it in a stained glass window to his memory in Trinity Church. A tablet could be erected for a comparatively few pounds, and if the rest of the money, or even the interest of it, were devoted to say, scholarships in connection with the Technical School, the memorial would be a benefit for all time.

I must say that, whatever is attempted, I trust there will be no such failure in carrying out the pro- ject as that which attended the proposed memorial to the late Mr. William Beamont. It is altogether a discredit to that section of the people of Warring- ton who have profited so much by Mr. Beamont's beneficent gifts that the scheme to perpetuate his memory utterly collapsed. I know that a number of people did subscribe, but nothing was done because the committee were not active either in subscribing or in doing anything else. They cer- tainly did incur a few small debts. Those debts have not yet been cleared off, and, unless the com- mittee take upon themselves to meet the accounts which are out-standing against them, these debts will be the only memorial they have raised to Mr. Beamont.

I I must say lam a little disappointed with the new bandstand in the park. I think that it is somewhat too heavy, and that it ought to be more lightsome in character to be in harmony with the purpose for Which it was built. Ido not like the dull chocolate colour of that part of the structure forming the enclosure within which the band will bit. Both on account of its height and its being of solid compact material, it almost hides the bands- men from view. Low iron railings painted green would have been much better, and more cheerful looking. As I listened to the strains of the band emanating from the enclosure, on Saturday after- noon, I was much pleased, but when I cast m 3 eyes on that unsightly part of the building my pleasure was by no means enhanced.

Alderman Burgess must have been considerably surprised when he read in the agenda of the last meeting of the Council and saw Councillor Roberts's motion in favour of the principle of dividing the work of the Sanitary Committee; and he was per- haps more surprised at the adoption of that motion by the Council. It almost seems as if, though Alderman Burgess will not go away from the cora- mittee,he will be likely to find the committee going away from him—for the plan proposed, if carried out,must involve some change in the chairmanship. It would have been interesting for the Alderman to have been present, and to have known his feelings when Mr. Roberts enunciated his revolutionary proposal, and found that there was a danger of the old Sanitary Committee.on which he prided himself so much, and the preservation .of the indivisible integrity of which must be a sacred mtitter to him, splitting up under his feet as it were, and in the splitting up leaving him—well in a position of "greater freedom and less responsibility."

I am sorry to read in the report of the Council meeting that difficulties are experienced in the ob- tainment of St. James's disused burial ground Its a place of recreation for the inhabitants of Latch ford. It seems, too, that if the acquisition is made, alto .most that the Council are likely to do in the way of met amorphosising the place is to convert it into an asphalted promenade, perhaps with a flower bed in the middle. Alderman Chandley thought that the conversion of the ground into a flower garden would be out of keeping with the character of the neighbourhood. I cannot see how the neigh hour- hood can be unsuitable. One would suppose that being so thickly populated it would be all the more. likely a quarter tor flower beds to be desirable %IQ to be appreciated.

, But I do not think flower beds coast-Atilt,. any essential part of a recreation ground, and there are plenty of such places in existence where there are no such beds. The most modest description of recre- ation ground, however, that I know of is certainly something more than an asphalted area—the somt, thing like, a skating rink—with a bed of flovrere the middle. Latchford will become more anti more urban as time goes on; and some consideration might be devoted to its future as well as to its pre- sent interests. Why not, if the ground is acquire!, preserve the grass, and plant a few ornain-ntiaa , shrubs, and put a few seats round the place? Coun- cillor Bolton thinks a caretaker would be necessary for flower beds', but there is no necessity to'have over one such bed—there are plenty of pleasant recreation grounds without these accessories—aril indeed without them there is all the larger space available for promenading.

I wonder if Free Education will ever become r.n accomplished fact in Earlestown. lam afraid n,r, unless the parents put their foot down, ant they will have it by hook or by crack. All ..,orts f red herrings are being drawn across the scent t deter the people from claiming what is due to hem by right ; but I would strongly ad vise them to bear in mind that the so-called difficulties exist only in the imagination of those who are intere.q.e.l in t,,e! management of the schools. If you want yoUr chi:- dren educated free, tell the schoolmaster or :chool- mistress Sc, and if they decline to grant your re- quest, then complain to the Education Depart ra-tit, and the matter will soon be put square. T oi• school authorities seem to be taking ath ft. tage of the apathy of the parents, and inatead of complying with the Act of Parliament they are • setting it at defiance, and attempting to Lai:tease the school fees, whenever they can find an oppor- tunity of doing it, without very much diffiadtv. What is the use of a law for the benefit of tlie people if it is to be ignored P I only hope that.. next Session the Act will be greatly amended.
MERLIN.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DANGEROUS FIREWORK PRACTICR.

At the borough magistrates' court yesterday, Ernest Leather, Wellfield-street, and John Ratcliffe, 233, Liver- pool-road, lads, were charged with discharging fireworks en tne 7th inst., in Liverpool-road, and also with damag- ing the door of a house, No. 79, Liverpool-road. Mr. Forshaw from the office of Messrs. P. Davies and Forshaw prosecuted.—Mr. Irian), of Thewlis-street, the owner of the property said the lads had destroyed the door to the extent of £2 18s. They had come to him, and said one of them had put a fire- work to the aoor and the other had set a match to it. The door had been so damaged that a new one would have to be provided, and the lock had been destroyed.— Wm. Siddle deposed to the damage to the door on the 7th inst., and said greater damage had been done to it the previous week in the same way. On the 7th a cracker was put into the keyhole and lit. —lnspector Spinks gave evidence as to the damage.— Matthias Spy said Leather told him that he put a Chinese squib in the keyhole. Leather's father said Chinese crackers were 20 for a penny and could not do much damage. They burnt like tissue paper, but did not blaze. The door was burnt round the lock, but there was not much damage done.—lnspector Spinks exploded one of the crackers in court, and it gave a somewhat loud report ; 6ut did not blaze.—The defend- ants were ordered to pay £1 damages, and the costs, 16s.

SATCRDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess, Mr. Geddes, and Mr. L. Voisey. _ _ _

- "A SHORT-SIGHTED Beresford was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Wilderspool-road, at a quarter-past eight on Friday night.—P.C. Hardy stated that he saw the defendant drive the horse attached to his cart on to the gates at the level crossing, in Wilderspool. One of the gates was forced open, and the animal was within an ace of falling in front cf a passing train.—The defendant pleaded that his pony was a little short-sighted, and was not aware of the gate. He admitted having imbibed a small quan- tity of beer.—Fined ss. and costs. _

div.head: E. J. Guest.
div.p: E. J. Guest.

THEFT OF A SKlRT.—Peter :ggins was charged with stealing a skirt, value 25., the property of Annie Ryan, also with assaulting her, the previous day. The Chief Gonstable said the complainant was a single woman, and the prisoner was known as a cornerrnan.—The prosecutrix said she, Alice Thomas, and the prisoner were drinking in a beerhouse in Mersey-street, and as their money was gone she was going home. He said " sell your skirt," and she refused, and he tore it off her to sell it to get more drink. She said " give me my skirt back," and he said he would not, and gave hcr a kick instead. He afterwards met her in Academy-street, and "leathered" her there.—Alice Thomas corroborated, and said the prisoner tried to sell the skirt at clothes dealers', but they would not have it, as they knew whose it was.—Mary Leslie, Mersey-street, deposed to her refusing to buy the skirt from the prisoner, because the button was missing and it looked as though it had been snatched off.—Joseph James, manager at the Legh Arms public-house, said the prisoner left a parcel there. —DS. Monaghan said he received from the last witness the parcel containing the skirt, after apprehending the prisoner, who told him where it was.—The prisoner to Monaghan: You are only proud of it, that's what it is.—He was committed to prison for two months' hard labour.—Alice Thomas was then called and catechised by the Chief Constable as to why she had not left the town the previous week, on condition of her doing which she was discharged.—She said a Mrs. Shepherd had been keeping her for a week.—The court missionary said he had got Mrs. Shepherd to keep her a few days, and in the meantime found there was a vacancy for her in the Shelter at Liverpool. She promised to go, but when he went to Mrs. Shepherd's found she had gone away but not to the shelter.—Thomas was rebuked by the Chair- man ror her conduct, and then allowed to stand down. EDUC.ATION CASES.—The following persons were dealt with on charges of not sending children regularly to school :—William Hickey, fish dealer, Wellfield-st., John James, joiner, Gladstone-St.,, whose son the Chairman allowed the alternative of going to the Clio, having a birching, or going to school,and who said he would go to school, Joseph Kirkham, forgeman, Catherine-st., sum- moned for the ninth time ; John McDonald,wire drawer, Rose and Crown-st., Richard Ridgeway, joiner, Sharpe- st., James Ward, labourer, Ship Yard, Joseph Wilcock, file cutter, Lord Nelson-st. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), and Alderman Wright. TUEFT 9F MEAT.—Annie Quinn was charged with stealing, the previous day, Gibs. of meat, the property of Maria Preston, butcher, Buttermarket-st. She was seen by Detective-Sergeant Monaghan watching the shop of Mr. Carlile, butcher, with something bulky under her shawl, and he discovered that it was the meat stolen from Mrs. Preston's. The prisoner was sent to jail for a month with hard labour. BREACH OF TUE EDUCATION ACT.—Thomas Moody, forgenian, Pierpoint-st., who had been summoned 16 times for not sending his children to school, and who now appeared under a warrant issued the previous day, was charged by Mr. G. Riley, School Attendance Officer, with not sending three children regularly to school. There were several old fines due from the defendant.— He was now fined ss. for each child, in default 7 days' imprisonment in each case. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John White was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., on the

previous night, also with assaulting his wife Bridget.— P. C. Clough said he heard screams of murder coming from the defendant's house and went in and found him drunk, and she complained that he had been assaulting her and threatening to stab her with a knife. After witness came out he waited about to see if the defendant assaulted her again, and he did so, and he was then taken into custody, and was very violent on the way to the station.—Mrs. White said her husband kicked her twice, but did not use his fist, and she asked for a sepa- ration order, and an allowance of 10s. per week.—The order was granted with an allowance of Bs. a week, and the defendant was sent to jail for a month with hard labour.

_ THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman), Alderman Sutton, Mr. John Fairclough, and Captain Ridgway. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—John Cain, 4, Oxford-street- Widnes, was charged with cruelty to a horse, by work log the same while in an unfit state, on the 28th Sept.— Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., proved the case.—The defendant said he had sold the horse for 10s., to a man who said he was going to knacker it.—A fine of 10s. was imposed.—John Hankey, of Orford, was charged by Mr. Dowty, with committing a like offence on the 30th ult.-20s. and costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Reynolds and Mr. C. Reynolds. ONLY ONCE.—Walter White, of 2, Trinity-street, was summoned for keeping a carriage without a license. The case wa,s proved by Wm. Speechley, Inland Revenue officer. The defendant said the trap had previously been the property of a a baker, and the only occasion on which he had used it, he was seen by Mr. Speechley.— He was ordered to pay the license (153.) and costs, Bs. 6d.

OVERCROWDED LODGING-HOUSES. - Thomas Kelly, Fryer-st. ; Michael Phillips, Mersey-st. ; Thos. Murphy, Mersey-st. ; and Mary Murphy, Fryer-st., lodging-house keepers, were summoned at the instance of the Board of Commissioners, with receiving into a certain room in their respective houses a greater number of lodgers than had been fixed as the maximum number by the Sanitary Authority. Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted. Tames Percival, the nuisance inspector, proved the cases. Kelly, who had recently been fined several times for other offences against the Sanitary regulations,was fined Eland costs ; Phillips was fined 103. and costs; and the two Murphy's were each fined ss. and costs. WITFMEtAWN.-Wm. Foster, of 19, Robert-street, was summoned for unlawfully assaulting Rebecca Basley. The summons was allowed to be withdrawn.

Cook,manager, said he would not be at all anxious to press the case, but they had been so intensely annoyed by lads coming into the works to pick cinders.
