div.head: DEATH OF A WA.RBINetTONIAN
div.p: DEATH OF A WA.RBINetTONIAN
IN AMERICA.

News has been received from America of the death of Mr. Thomas Moulding, who was a native of Warrington. The "Chicago Morning News Record" of September 21st, gives the following obituary notice of the deceased :—" One of Chicago's oldest and best-known workers in the cause of temperance is dead. Thomas Moulding, one of the founders of the Washingtonian and Martha Wash- ington homes, died early yesterday morning at Buena Vista, Col., after a sickness of several weeks' duration. Mr. Moulding had taken his wife to Colorado in hopes that her health would be benefitted by the change. They left Chicago in the early part of June, sojourning at Colorado Springs. The first intimation that the family had of Mr. Moulding's bad health was conveyed to them in a letter received by Dr. W. P. Goodsmith, a son-in•law, from a physician in Colorado Springs, which told of the serious nature of the sick man's malady, and advised that some member of the family come on at once. Dr. Goodsmith arrived at Mr. Moulding's bedside last Saturday. He was much better, and, as a result of a consultation of physicians, he was removed to Buena Vista, where it was thought the springs would help him. From the time of his removal there was a gradual decline until his death. Thomas Moulding was born in Warrington, England, Dec. 13, 1825. He learned the trade of machinist and early de- veloped an unusual interest in temperance work. While in England, he together with ler. P. P. Carpenter and other eminent men succeeded in doing much good among the working people. In 1851 he came to America and located in Carpenterville, 11l , where he worked at his trade. A few years latter he moved to Chicago, where he has since resided. Mr. Moulding in 1861 for- sook the machine-shop and commenced the manufacture of brick. Moulding and Harland was the firm's name until 1879, when Mr. Harland withdrew from the firm. Dr. Moulding was one of the founders of the Citizen's league and has been a trustee of the Wash- ingtonian home since its inception. He was a member of the Unity church as long as the Rev. Dr. Robert Collyer remained its pastor, and then joined the Wesley Methodist church, of which he was a trustee at the time of his death. Mr. Moulding was also much interested in educational matters, and for twelve years was a member of the Lake View school board before the annexation. Among his friends he was known as one of the most upright of men, and a great part of his life was spent in lifting unfortunates from the slums and placing them in a position to earn an honest living. Be was an old member of the Sons of Temperance of both the Illinois and national divisions and also a member of the Good Tempters. Mr. Moulding leaves a wife and five children. Mrs. W. P. Goodsmith, Lizzie, Thomas Jr., Joseph and Pearl Moulding. Invitations were out for the marriage of Miss Lizzie Moulding to Dr. Heber Newton Goodsmith, which event was to have occurred on Sept. 27, but the death of Mr. Moulding bas occas- ioned the recall of the invitations. The remains will be brought back tc Chicago for burial."

div.head: FttWERAL.
div.p: THE FttWERAL.

The' Chicago Tribune" of Sep 24th, contains the following :—Many of the friends of Thomas Moulding gathered at the Wesley M.E. Church on North Halsted- street yesterday afternoon to hear the Rev. N. H. Axtell utter the last words of condolence to the bereaved family. After a brief service at the residence, No. 957 North Clark-street, the funeral procession proceeded to the church, where the Rev, N. H. Axtell, assisted by the Revs. J. C. Staughton and H. Johnson, conducted the services. The plain black casket was strewn with tributes of friends, among which a large pillow from the Builders' Exchange and a "gates ajar" from the officers of the Washington Home were conspicuous. Dr. Axtell in his sermon spoke of the noble work which Mr. Moulding was instrumental in carrying through. At its meeting yesterday afternoon the Citizens' League of Chicago adopted the following regarding the death of Thomas Moulding The Citizens' League of Chicago deeply feels the loss it has sustained in the death of Thomas Moulding. He was one of the eight persons by whom the league was founded in the hall of the Garden City Division of the Sons of Temperance, November 25th, 1877, and was one of its most faithful and zealous supporters until the day when he was called to his eternal reward. He was a member of the Executive Committee of this league and a veteran in its service in that capacity, and was also, at the time of his death, a member of the Committee of the World's Congress Auxiliary on the Temperance Con- gresses to be held at Chicag.) in 1893. As a member of the Executive Board, by which the affairs of the league are administered, he was noted for the regularity of his attendance, his interest in the work of the league,and his fidelity and zeal in prosecuting that work, to practical and substantial results. Side by side with P. F. Elnendorf and Andrew Paxton he kept the faith and waged the fight of law and order for the protec- tion of the boys of Chicago against the seductions of in- 1 temperance, vice, and crime. He is entitled to a just share of the honors and blessings which the league has won in all the victorious campaigns of the last fifteen years. Mr. Moulding was also a member of other or- ganisations formed to protect society and advance the general welfare, and we may properly leave to them the recognition of his valuable services in the fields in which they are engaged. But affection and duty unite in ask- ing at our hands this tribute to his worth in the cause in which our effmrts are devoted. It is, therefore, , ordered, that this memorial minute be entered at large in the record of the league ; that a copy thereof be sent to the family of our deceased brother ; and that a copy be also furnished to the public Press in testimony of the esteem in whibi. Thomas Moulding was held by his asso- ciate S Of the Citizens' Leagno of Chicago.

The strike at Borinage, in e Mons district of Belgium is spreaning, and on Thursday morning 3,800 men had left work. Thirteen persons have been seriously injured, one of them it is feared fatally, by a colliAion on the Sixth- avenue elevated railroad at 125th Street, New York.

WIDNES V. MOSSLEY A. TEAMS—Played at Widnes, and ended in a draw, no points being scored. RUNCORN A. V. WIDNES ST. MARY'S—Played at Run- corn, Oil Saturday, and the home team woo by two tries to one, fluxcome v. TIJEBROOK.—A poor team of Runcorn players owing to county demands, turned out at Tue- brook on Saturday, on their first engagement. The Runcornians won the toss, and took advantage of the slope, but the home lot early got under weight, and following a lengthy stay in their 25 quarters, Eccles registered a minor point from an unsuccessful drop at goal. After the drop out the play progressed evenly, some good passing on the part of Eccles and Battersby being nipped by the capital tackling of the visitors' backs. The home side, h )wever, not to be denied, again attacked, but only a minor point followed. when Run- corn had a f sir chance from a penalty kick, but nothing accrued up to half-time. On turning round the play be- came keener,but scoring seemed out of the question,and the game resulted in a draw of two minor points each. RUNCORN v. OLD WirrbruANs.—This mitch, played at Nerthwich on Saturday, proved moat interesting. The teams turned out as follows :—Runcorn: Goal, Main- ' waring ; full backs, Higson and Fisher; half backs, A. Limb, Richards, and Pope; forwards, Limb, Garvie, Wright, Bates, and Whiteman. Old Wittonians : Goal, Goodwin ; full backs, Whitlow and Thomas; half backs, Warburton, Barker, and Tweedie ; forwards, Shaw, Marrow, Ryan, Sands, and Bates. Runcorn winning the toss kicked off down hill, and quickly pressed, but met with a severe repulse, the ball soon travelling back to- wards the visitors' goal. Shortly after this Limb got away, and shooting low and quick scored the first point, Ryan for the home side shortly after equalizing. These proved the only points scored in the first half, and the teams crossed over on equal terms. On resumiag, play was very even, when, from a pass by Marrow, Shaw gave the home team the lead with a well-placed shot. Soon afterwards, Limb was conspicuous with a useful sprint, passing both the home backs and centreing well. Whiteman equalized again with an easy shot. The home team then pressed hotly to get the desired winning point, but their efforts were fruitless against the sound defence of the visitors' backs, and a pleasant game ended in a draw of two goals each. EAST v. WEST CHESHIRE. The game between picked teams of the East and West Division of Cheshire came off on Saturday, at Liscard, before a very fair attendance of spectators. There were several alterations from the original selec- tion, as will be seen from the following list :—Probables —F. S. Edwards, (New Brighton), back ; H. Ashton, (Stockport), J. H. Crompton (Runcorn), and P. R. Clause, (Birkenhead Park), three-quarter backs; F. Drinkwater, (Sale), and S. Abrams, (Rancorn), half- backs ; P. Riley, 0. Fiughes, A. Hampson, (Runcorn) ; A. J. Chadwick, (Birkenhead Park) ; W. A. William's, (New Brighton), W. B. Smith, (New Brighton), E. Elliott, (Birkenhead Wanderers), Moss, (Dukinfield), and Speet, (Stockport), forwards. Possibles—J. T. Haslam, (Stockport), back ; F. Saville, (Stockport), W. Fleet, (Altrincham), C. Kelly, (Birkenhead Wanderers), three-quarter backs; ft. S. Thorpe, (Sale), and H. Morris, (Stockport), half-backs ; Bennett (Dukinfield), E. H. Potts,(Stockport). W. Stephens, (Sale), W. J Tyack, (Dukinfield), F. Little, (New Brighton), H. Williams,(Runcorn), J. Davies, (Runcorn), J. Davies, (Runcorn), F. H. Smith, (Birkenhead Park), J. Gardiner Birkenhead Wanderers. The Probables opened the game, and, following some give-and-take play round the central line, Keenly punted to Clauss, and following the punt Saville ran grandly, and with Gardhzer took the play to the Probables' line. A free kick relieved, and then the whole line, headed by Hughes, dribbled the length of the ground, Kelly lust racing up in time to save his side. Crompton had a chance, but lost com- mand of his feet, and the Possibles by a series of short dribbles took the play to midfield. Here Ashton got possession, but skated Hong Mother Earth, and later on Saville was tackled off side, and the Possibles gained further headway. The sodden state of the ground was responsible for many funny incidents, and eventually Crompton was collared with the ball near his line, and when matters looked promising for the Possibles, Ashton ran round his line and sent into touch at his 25. From the line out the ball was sent over the line, when Edwards timely stepped in and saved disaster at the expense of a minor point. Dropping out, midfield became the scene of hostilities. Fleet made his mark, but Edwards returned, and after a few somer- saults Crompton put in some capital dodging, to which the Possibles' front rank retaliated with a strong rush to within a few yards of their opponents' line. An inter- cepted pass gave the needful relief, but still the Possi- bles were net to be denied, and again attacked, and dribbling on, the ball was taken over the line, only to be saved by Riley. Following the drop out Saville feinted to pass, but eventually sent on to Kelly, and the Wan- derer, from a difficult position, dropped unmistakably over the bar, thus scoring first blood in the game. From the centre kick the Pronables paid a visit to the other end, where Little intercepted a pass, and thus prevented further inroad, and, just as the Possibles' forwards were getting into a good stride, the whistle was blown for half time, the score standing.—Possibles 1 goal and 2 minors ; Probables, nil. On restarting the Whites were again early in evidence, and a minor point was notched. Kelly saved a strong rush at the other end, and, follow- ing up his kick, got possession of the ball, and set up a capital movement, which brought matters to the Stripes line, where Edwards timely saved. Williams, Smith, and Riley gave relief, when Kelly got possession and contributed a splendid run, and just as scoring seemed certain the Probable back kicked dead. Another minor point resulted from a strong rush of the whites. Little put in some capital forward work, and Saville and Kelly were again busy in attack. Williams broke through and took the play to the centre. W. B. Smith made further headway. Haslam saving splendidly. A moment later Clause gained possession, and sending on registered a minor point for the stripes. A couple of free kicks to the Probables proved fruitless, Clause, who had not been too well attended to, put in a Capital single-handed effort, but time was called quickly afterwards, leaving the Possibles winners by a goal to nil.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. LANCASTER.

The first meeting of these clubs this season took place at Wilderspool on Saturday. Inclement weather again prevailed, but, as was the case a week previous, a game worthy of the reputation of the two clubs was performed, the spectaters occasionally being worked up to a high pitch of enthusiasm. Lancaster rought their best team, whilst on the home side, Evans re-appeared at half-back. There would be over 3,000 present when Lancaster kicked off towards the pavilion gaol, and although the initial item brought about the Warrington quarter being invaded, Boscow was soon eased of his responsibility, Heesom judiciously kicking to near the half-way. Pass- ing by the home half-backs saw Plumpton further im- proving the Warringtonians' position, and, although Garth followed the precedent set him by Bate and Evans with a short pass to Danby, the latter was soon bored before he could clear. Evans next dallied with a pass to Webster, but a moment later amends were made when Evans again dodged round a pack ; and tricking the half-backs and three-quarters in a clever manner, he easily accounted for Cowell, and Heesom was called upon to place an easy goal. A fine return by Plumpton again placed Lancaster on their defence, Hartley failing to reply. Another beautiful display by the Warrington backs was this time staved off at the right moment, but , Turner, Jolley, and Donohue disputed the right to posi- tion, and the homesters consequently maintained their footing in Lancaster quarters. Getting the better of a pack the Northerners relieved slightly, Ashton checking them at half way, but Webster with his usual kick and quick following up soon regained the lost position. Not to be denied, the visitors forced the game beyond the half way flag, whilst further ground was obtained when Bleasdale, Danby, and Garth passed, and Boscow was called upon to defend. Turner, Elolmes, and Thorniley headed Warrington back to mere desirable quarters, whilst on a couple of occasions Jolley looked extremely dangerous, only the safe tackling of Bleasdale prevent- ing the county forward from crossing the border. Turner took a pass well from the latter, which led up to Plump- ton being held near the line. The oval was again got out of danger by the brothers Wilson, and Warrington ' now showed up to perfection in the dribbling art, when Donohue and Holmes came away from the ruck, and the latter crossing to Bate, that player was a foot forward. and the opportunity was lost. The free kick did not avail the Lancaster men much, for the next item saw Bate running down the open, and passing across to Thorniley. This player made no mistake, and the score was augmented to the tune of two points, Evans failing at the place. A spell of free kicks claimed attention soon after the drop out, if anything Lancaster having the better of the exchanges. Donohue, Teare, and Heesoin got dangerously near the visitors' lines, but Cowell drove them back, and a couple of rushes by the forwards were met with confidence by Webster and Plumpton. The determined attack of Lancaster was eventually cleared by Webster, and the same player was loudly applauded a minute later in tak- ing a pass from Heesom. Kicking well, he followed up and Handles being handy and Hartley missing, the War- rington forward gave the charge to Webster once more, far that player to canter in an easy scorer, Heesom again doing the needful with the place. Nothing daunted by this last reverse, the visitors still played up hopefully, and a sequence of passes certainly deserved something tangible. lleesom stepped in, and taking the oval got it away to centre. Plumpton was here conspicuous for a tackle of Bleasdale, and though Danby got within measurable distance of the Warrington line, the interval arrived with the homesters leading by two goals and a try to nil. No time was lost in commencing the second half, but the fast pace which marked the opening half had had its effect, and the play toned down considerably. In fact, the first twenty minutes were monopolised by forward play, and the monotony was only relieved by some sharp passing by the home backs, which had a futile effect. Lancaster continued to have slightly the best of this half, and despite the fact that Heesom con- tinually cleared his lines, the visitors could not be held at bay. Their persistency was at length rewarded, for B. Thompson got over near the posts, and Denby placed a goal. The game now underwent a remarkable change, for the homesters being awakened to their responsibility put forth their best endeavours, and, as a consequence, Cowell was busily defending ids charge. Webster made a fine effort, which led up to an earnest attack, but the climax was reached when Bate, Evans, and Heesom ran and passed magnificently, and the centre giving up the oval to Plumpton, the latter completed the afternoon's score with a clever try, Turner this time failing at the place, Final score : Warrington, 2-2-1; Lancaster 1-0-1.

• Teams :—Warrington oscow, back ; Plutnpton, ileesom, and Webster, three-quarters ; John Bate and Evans, half-backs ; 11. Ashton, Fair Turaer, Jolley, Bandies, Thornilcy, Holmes, Donohue, Teare, and Griffiths, forwards. Lancaster : Cowell, back; Hartley, Bleasdale, and Lambert, three-quarters ; Garth and Danby, half-backs ; T. Gibson, C. Gibson, Herbert, E. Thompson, B. Thompson, Carter, Kitchen, Barnett, and Lofthouse, forwards. WARRINGTON A v. LANCASTHR A.—After the miser- ably wet weather experienced in this locality of late, the beautifully fine day at Lancaster was a treat, so that the encounter was witnessed by the usual expect- ant crowd. The visiting team were at once in evidence, smart passing between their hacks carrying the leather ta the line. Offside play by Warrington was duly pen- alized, but Lally, Barnes, and Lawless, by capital runs, gained a great advantage for their side. Then Hartley relieved his lines splendidly, and, following some equal play in neutral territory, Ashurst punted to touch well into his opponents' 25. Clever play by Lally and Smith was supplemented by Hampson, Davies, Molyneaux, and Bailey rushing to goal. Here Leake got grandly away, but Ashurst floored him in grand style at the half-way line. Lally was the medium by which Smith made a splendid run, Lawless, after a similar effort, being only pulled up on the line by Hartley. The game was of the fastest character, the ball travelling rapidly about the field, but ultimately Edwards dashed away to the Lancaster line, a minor being conceded ' shortly afterwards. Following the drop out, Barnes, Ashurst, and Daniels put in some capital work, but the home team retaliated bi rushing into their antagonists' quarters, and for a time pressed. Bradbury cleared, and then a beautiful display of running and passing by Lally, Smith, Barnes, and Edwards took the warfare to the other end of the ground. When half-time came nothing had been scored. Lancaster restarted the con- test, the first item of note being a capital run by Smith ; and some dashing play by Antrobus, Molyneux, and Fligham, took the ball in close proximity to the line. A dash by Ralph and Gardiner removed the danger, but the leather was soon hovering round the home goal posts, which had a lucky escape, and a minor resulted. Antrobus's return and Lally's sprint again harrassed the Lancaster deLmce, but a strong pressure wss subsequently relieved. While both sets of forwards were contesting every inch of ground at the centre line, Lally stole splendidly away, and, :rimming grandly, eluded Hartley and scored between the posts, Barnes converting. After this Lancaster got inta the Warring- ton quarters, Ashurst only stopping Lambert on the line when a try seemed certain. Then Lancaster had a shat at goal from a free kick, Lawless getting the oval finely away. The home team returned to the attack, Antrobus came through to the 25,and Lally, and Daniels. taking the ball clear to the Lancaster citadel, but a minor was all that could be obtained. Warrington had all the play afterwards, Lally workinClike a Trojan, and then after a brilliant flash of passing between Smith, Lally, Barnes, Antrobus, and ' Lawless, the ball was again secured by Lally, who threw across to Barnes,and a try obtained, Warrington winning by 1-1-5 to nil.

WARRINGTON 2ND T. WIDNES RANGERS.—PIayed at Warrington. on Saturday. Warrington kicked off and at once began to press. A long kick by Taylor was well followed up by H. Thornton, who had hard lines in not scoring,a minor being the result from the drop-out. The Rangers rushed up the field, but Boldsworth relieved in splendid style. Gibson then showed up with a nice run and kick. The remainder of the first half was keenly contended. Score at half time, Warrington, P. minors to 1. Widnes kicked off, and Warrington charged down, Hartles saving. A pass intended for a Widnes man was taken by Barratt, who ran in under the post, but the referee did not allow the point. Not to be denied, War- rington again attacked and had extremely hard lines, Taylor being held on the line twice in succession. Time was called shortly after, leaving the game drawn, 2 minors each. The Warrington team included some new blood, viz :—Boldsworth at full back, who played a splendid game throughout. The pick of the forwards were Barratt, Monks, and H. Thornton, who played an untiring game. Warrington 2nd team.—Full back, Boldsworth; three-quarter backs, Taylor, Speakman, Jackson, Gibson; half-backs, Rowe, captain, Griffiths; forwards, W. Barratt, H. Thornton, J. Thornton, F. Monks, J. Quinn, Warburton, Russell, Woods.

WARRINGTON RANGERS V. RUNCORN RECREATION.— Played at Warrington, on Saturday. The Recreation kicked off, but off-side play brought them back. The homesters carried the scrimmage and Price kicked strongly, a minor accruing. rhe Recreation played up, and almost scored after good passing, but the Rangers' defence left nothing to be desired. The game was of an interesting character, both teams displaying good foot- ball, but with the exception of a minor to each side nothing was recorded up to half time. Clarke re- started, and a fine passing run by the visitors' baeks took play to the home quarters, where the game for some time was stubbornly contested. Eventually, the homesters got clear, Clare obtaining possession, and after a short run threw to Potts, who effected a fine run in the kick at goal failing. From the drop out the Recreation by good play gained ground. The game now became very fast and exciting, Potts and Holt running in additional tries, and the Rangers finally proved ;he victors by one goal, two tries, three minors to Runcorn one minor.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

SANDBACH SCHOOL V. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL. —This match was played on the ground of the tormer on Saturdayrand resulted in a win for Sandbach by seven goals to one. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION RESERYR V. APPLETON RAN- °HRS.—These teams met at Arpley. Appleton kicked off against the wind, and after several corners, which were badly placed, Parrott scored from a bit of neat passing. Play was now of a give-and-take kind, but eventually the visitors scored from a miskick. Thomp- son next scored with a grand shot, placing Warrington ahead at half-time by two goals to one. Restarting, the visitors played well up, and were not long in equalizing. From some good passing on the part of the Appleton forwards, the visitors scored a soft goal after having a fruitless penalty kick, Qom which the ball rebounded after striking the posts into play. Warrington still pressing, their final efforts were weak in front of goal, until Radford getting possession equalized for the home- sters. After some splendid play by the visitors they drew ahead, the whistle sounding soon after, ending a good game, by Appleton Rangers four goals. Warring- ton Reserve, three goals.

div.head: CORPSE FOUND IN A DRAIN AT RAINFORD.
div.p: A CORPSE FOUND IN A DRAIN AT RAINFORD.

- - --- - Considerable excitement prevails in Rainford, near St. Helens, in consequence of a horrible dis- covery in Rainford Churchyard. For about two months the lower portion of the graveyard has been flooded, the drain having got choked with tree roots. To open the drain most of the trees had to be cut down. While assisting in the work Sexton Joseph Green saw a box protruding from some rubbish, and on examination the decomposed body ot a child was found, wrapped in red flannel. Dr. Brooks, police sergeant for Rainford district, states that it is the body of a fully-developed child, but on account of the decomposition be is unable to make any declaration as to the cause of death. The box is supposed to have been there for some month., it being the most unfrequented Dart of the churchyard. Mr. Brighouse has been communi- sated with.

FOOTBALL.

The clubs who contemplate taking part in the Lanca- shire Rugby Cup Competition of next season have sent in their names, and it now remains for the County Com- mittee to meet and classify the clubs into divisions, so that the competition may be successfully floated. No less than thirty-five organisations have signified their intention of competing, but Manchester, Liverpool, and Liverpool Old Boys have not thought proper to enter. The committee will have a very dolicate task in making the distinction and estimating the merits of the compe- titors. There will be three classes of ten each, and the oddment of five will form another division. The follow- ing is a list of the clubs entered : Swinton Aspull Salford Manchester Rangers Warrington Blackley Oldham Blaekley Rangers Wigan Leigh Tvldesley Boothstown St. Helens Crompton St. Helens Recreation Radcliffe Rochdale Hornets Pendleton Broughton Rangers Werneth Lancaster Pemberton Ulverston Barton Barrow Tottington Broughton Free Wanderers Walkden Swinton Hornets Mossley Widnes St. Mary's Rochdale St. Clement's Stalybridge Widnes

"Smack" Bate will, it is expected, be sufficiently re- covered from his accident to play for Warrington against Oldham to-day, Warrington being due at Watershed- dings in their first League engagement with the Oldham team.

On Saturday two important games in the Lancashire , Rugby Cup Competition were decided—or rather, I should say were contested—without any major point being scored. Considering that the four clubs were the great rivals in their respective districts, this result is all the more curious. In the Salford-Swinton match two minors each were scored, and in the Ilreughton-Brough- ton Rangers game the latter claim whatever ascendancy may be gained from having three minors to their credit.

And in connection with this latter fact a difficulty has arisen. The Rangers contend that, according to the rules of the competition (rule 7), they are entitled to claim a victory, for it is laid down in the code of rules of the contest that " in the event of no major points being scored, or of the major points being equal, a minor point conceded in defence (that is, last touched by the defending side) shall count one point, and a majority of three such points shall constitute a win."

The thousand-and-odd supporters of the St. Helens Recreation who accompanied the team to Tyldesley last Saturday, were says the " Athletic News," mightily pleased to be witnesses of the well-won victory of their pets. Those who saw the match were quite convinced that the St. Helens " Rees' "team is stonger and more perfect this season, than at any previous period of the club's existence. Never until Saturday have the " Rees "been able to defeat the " Bongers "on their own ground, and the difficulty of the task only enhances the victory.

Tyldesley are expecting to join the Lancashire Cup Competition this season, and this knowledge made them strive the harder to beat their sturdy opponents, but all in vain. Seeing that Swinton the other week, on their own ground, only got the better of Tyldesley by a single try—the only one of the match—the " Rees" may be fairly congratulated on their very promising entrance into the competition. They are very confident in the glass-making; town that St. Helens Recreation will, at the end of the present season, be found among the first three in th list.

Several of the League games on Saturday last proved wonderfully attractive to the sport-loving public. This was especially the case at Everton, where the gate was a bumper, whilst there was also a splendid gathering at Nottingham and a big assemblage at Preston. From the following figures it will be seen that the seven matches averaged close upon 10,000 spectators each : _
, Everton v. Sunderland Notts County v. Notts Forest

Preston North Hnd v. Blackburn Rovers. 10,000 , Newton Heath v. West Bromwich Albion. 8 000 Burnley v. Derby County 7,000 Wolverhampton Wanderers v. Aston Villa 6,000 Accriugton•. Bolton Wanderers 4,000

Two of the results must be counted as genuine sur prises. The first of these was the very pronounced vic- tory of the champions. When they were last at Everton they astonished the Liverpudlians by taking them down four goals to nothing. On Saturday, Sun- derland were expected to have all their work cut out, as Everton have been going great guns recently, but the latter were sadly outclassed. The Wearsiders treated the immense crowd to a superb display of football, and demonstrated their unrivalled ability by a victory of four goals to one.

This in the light of recent events stamps the Simder land team as a wonderful combination. Here they beat Evertun by three goals two days after the Liverpoo players had drawn with Queen's Park on the same ground. The inference is that the League cracks are vastly spperior to the Scotch amateurs, both pure and adulterated, seeing that on Thursday they visited the Celtic at Glasgow, and trotted them round by three goals to none. This was a splendid performance, even allowing that the Glasgow club were a man short in the second half.

The second of the Leaguer-surprises of Saturday wa the extent of the defeat of Notts Forest by their power' ful rivals, Notts County_ The contest was rendered doubly interesting frous the fact that this was the first League battle between the two clubs, a circumatanc e which doubtless accounted to some extent for the magni- ficent attendance. No one believed Notts County to be capable of defeating their neighbours by three goals, whilst they kept the Forest from scoring. It was a great victory.

Three of the seven League engagements terminated exactly alike, as will be seen below : Goals. Goals. Preston North End 2 Blackburn Rovers 1 Burnley .... . 2 Derby County 1 Wolverhampton Wands 2 Aston Villa The home club was in each case successful, from which it would appear that the teams are well matched, as the choice of ground is generally considered to be equal to a goal. All three were desperately stubborn games.and in two instances the result hung in tha balance until the end was within view.

Like Sunderland the North End enjoyed themselves at the week end. They easily accounted for the Third Lanark at Glasgow, and Saturday found them at home scoring one more League success against the Rovers. The popularity of the Blackburn club with the Preston- ians was seen in the excellent gate, which was the best recorded at Deepdale for some time. The Rovers invariably show up strongly when opposed to• the North End, and they gave the spectators plenty for their money. Preston were certainly thankful when the end arrived.

THE SCOTCH FISHERY DISTURBANCES.

A telegram from Berwick states that a Tweed bailiff was on Wennesday night attacked and roughly used by a mob, who afterwards stormed the lodge at Cam n Rock, "and poured paraffin down the chimney, order not being restored until after the arrival of the police.
AL A.RIIING EXPLOSION AT A. COLLIE Ea.

On Thursday morning a singular explosion took place in the smithy of Edge-lane Colliery, Oldham. Whilst a man was attending to the fire a terrible explosion oc- curred, seriously injuring three men and wrecking the place. The cause of the affair is not known.

div.head: BROMPTON MYSTERY.
div.p: THE BROMPTON MYSTERY.

The inquest on Miss Sharpe, otherwise known as " Ruby Russell, who was connected with what was called the Brompton mystery, was concluded on Thurs- daa, the jury finding that the decaased died from mor- phia poisoning, but expressing no opinion as to whether the poison was wilfully or accidentally administered. They added their opinion, however, that no suspicion rested upon Dr. Heron.
SERIOUS DEPRESSION IN THE STEEL TRADE.

Through bad trade and the absence of margin work has gradually been suspended in certain departments of the extensive concern belonging to the Bolton Iron and Steel Company,. Limited, and now about 400 men out of nearly seven hundred usually engaged have been stopped and there is no immediate prospect of improvement. Trade at the works is worse now than ever since their origin above fifty years ago.

div.head: SUSPECTED MURDER NEAR LONDON.
div.p: SUSPECTED MURDER NEAR LONDON.

The body of a man was found on Saturday in the Grand Junction Canal, near Willesden, by a bargeman named Frederick Morris. The throat was cut from ear to ear, and the. lower part of the body was terribly mutilated. The spot is a lonely one near 'I wyford Abbey, and some distance from any house.

div.head: EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.
div.p: EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.

The solicitor for the convict Banbury, who was sen- tenced to death at the last session of the Criminal Court for the murder of a youne; woman in Walworth, recently sent a petition to the Home Secretary praying for a commutation of the sentence, but the Home Secretary did not see his way to interfere with the sentence. John James Banbury was executed at Wandsworth Gaol at nine o'clock on TUesday morning. The culprit, who slept little during the night, was visited early in the morning by the prison, chaplain, to whom he expressed the deepest remorse. After being pinioned by Billingtion the unfortunate man walked tothe scaffold with much firmness, and deatbappeared tai be instantaneous.

div.head: YOUTHFUL JACK SHEPHERD&
div.p: YOUTHFUL JACK SHEPHERD&

Inquiries made by the county police authorities show that the boys committed at Bolton to the Manchester Assizes on suspicion of burglary have no connection with the mysterious shooting affair which took place at Fazakerley. From the evidence adduced at Bolton it appeared that four youths, named Richard Fielding, Thomas Hamer, John Rawcliffe, and J. W. Ratcliffe, had broken into an ironmonger's shop and stolen therefrom a number of revolvers with cartridges. While engaged in their depredations on the premises referred to they were interrupted by a Mr. Atherton, at whom they fired, missing their mark, however. Fielding was stated to be the leader of the juvenile ganF.t, and he,. it appears, ordered the others to make out of the town and shoot and rob some person. The boys had been evidently led into their mischievous conduct ' through reading" blood and thunder" tales. Hamer was discharged.

It appears that on his arrival at Czenstochowa, where a monument erected to Alexander 11. was to be unveiled by the Czar, two dynamite mines exploded on the side of the platform where thetrain was expected to stop. At the very last moment, nA it seems through a mistake made by a. signalman. 0.3 train Was shifted to another platform, thus prow i for the Czars mimeo!. ous escape. The mines, V fired by electricity, and five persons who had Ise( ..tanding near were killed on I the spot, whilst fourteer ,hers Were more or less severely injured. SHOCKING MURDER, AND A.TTENIPTED

SUICIDE. A shocking minder was committed at Honley, Huddersfield, on Monday. Wright Charles Littlewood, a size manufacturer, went upstairs, and his wife, vibe was in the kitchen, hearing screams, ran up, and BfIAV him with his throat cut, and holding a carving knife. She was horrified to see their crippled daughter Emily, aged 16, with her head nearly severed, and quite dead. Littlowood, who was arrested, was supposed to be suffering from delirium tremens. Liitlewood Was brought before the magistrates in the afternoon and remanded for eight days. The. prisoner, who is not much hurt, appeared almost indifferent to his terrible position, but glanced furtively around the court at times as if expecting to see sorn-one. The family was always regarded as a quiet one until lately, when Littlewood developed drinking habits.
BRITISH TROOPS..
CAUGHT IN AMBUSH.

SEVENTEEN KILLED. The following appears in the second edition of the 14 Times CALCUTT!S, October 13.—1 n the Northern. Chin Bills• a native officer's escort fell into an ambush, and 17 men were killed by the Chins it ..oc miles distance from Fort White. A small force commanded by Captain Garfield has started in search of the missing, bodies. The Chins having set fire to the village decamped, but are still lying in ambush within two miles of Fort white, and skirmishing is now in progress. A reinforcement, con- sisting of a mountain battery with 100 of the Ist Burmah Infantry and 200 of the Norfolk leaves Man- dalay for Fort White on Friday.

div.head: TEE LIFE SATING SOCIETY.
div.p: TEE LIFE SATING SOCIETY.

The above Society, founded last year for the tion of Technical Education in Life Saving and Besu tation of the apparently drowned, recently decided the final tie of the National Life Saving C)mpetition, for the Sunlight Challenge Shield, presented by Messrs. Lever Bros., Limited. The two teams left in the final were Nottingham No. 2 and Ravensbourne (Landon). Both seams were examined in private by Dr. Evans, of Liver- pool, who put both teams through a very severe trial,. testing them thoroughly in every part of the resuscita— tion movement, after the examination, punctual to time, both teams appeared and after a most interesting and exhaustive trial, the Nottingham team obtained the greater number of marks and thus became the first holders of the most valuable trophy in the swimming world, in addition to which each member of the Learn received a gold medal. The second team received silver medals and the winners of the penultimate rounds of the Northern and Southern District Competitions both received four bronze medals each, and the winners of the divisional contests not taking any of the above prizes, also received bronze med,ds, thus, in addition tø the Shield which is valued at £6O, twenty-four Gold, Silver, and Bronze Medals were given for the promotion of a knowledge which it is hoped will be of the highest advantage in cases of emergency. Result—Nottingham, Resuscitatien (Doctor's award) 7 points, Land Drills 25, Water Drills 33i, total 651. Ravensbourne, 6, 2.5; 20° respectively, total 58i The same evening there WaS also decided the Long Plunge Championship, which was. won by El. A. Wilson, J. M. Hugh was second, and E. Sandiford third. div.head: tenets to the Obitor.
div.p: tenets to the Obitor.
BAD LANGUAGE AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—The attention of the police might very well be .concentrated upon certain parts of our Runcorn (viz.) Church-st., Bridge-st., Cawley's-lane, and Norman-road, as to the shocking language used by a certain class of men and youths, while young girls and women are walking about these parts of the town. On Sunday last while walking round Cawley's-lane, I met a number of well-dressed lads who were shouting and whistling at passers-by, who were subjected to very vulgar and indecent remarks. I heard very foul lan- guage indulged in when two girls (about the age of seventeen or eighteen) passed. It will be a disgrace to the police if such a state of things is allowed to exist. Hoping you will kindly insert this, and that the pub- licity thus given, will be the means of putting an end to the *present discreditable state of affairs,—l am, Yours &c., Runcorn, October 10, 1892.
PRO BONO PUBLICO.
THE SAGE OF PENKETH ANENT THE GOOSE AND HIS BANTLING.

Sir,—lt must be as highly diverting to see the Sage of Penketh fiercely and furiously contending in arms against a goose, as it was formerly to find him patroniz- ing a red herring for a bantling. In either case the Sage has lost his temper and his dignity, and made a pitiable object in representing the stately march of evolution. It is also amusing to find him labour so strenuously to shift the point in dispute. I maintain that, if an Agnostic Evolutionist links man on to the lower animals by necessary and immutable law, then there is no reason why a different code of moral laws should apply to him. Those laws which regulate the lives of the lower animals should also apply to man. The Sage's defence of the claims ot the anti-vivisectionists,l regarded as inconsist- ent with this principle. In saying so, he makes me responsible for taking part with the vivisectionist. Such a claim is entirely without foundation ; and so far as I am concerned he is at liberty to attack them to his heart's content.

He also says that I precluded him from protesting against the maltreatment of the lower animals, because as an Evolutionist, he, as such, acknowledges kinship by descent" from his fellow beings." Now, I do not protest against him acknowledging" kinship by descent from his fellow beings :" what I protest against is his kinship " from " the lower animals, aye, even" from " the goose and red herring—animals lower in the scale of evolution, and for which he seems to have a special predilection. It is because he links man on to the lower animals in the same chain of necessary and immutable law that he has no right to separate man as a moral being. Moreover, if the laws regarding the struggle for existence and the survival of the fittest applr to man, then there is no reason why the Hospital and Infirmary should be built for the purpose of allevi- ating the sufferings of the weak and the dying ; nor is there any necessity for building the Lunatic Asylum for the protection of its inmates from the most terrible of diseases. The Agnostic Evolutionist, in order to be consistent, should destroy all such unfortunates by death. . _

There is also another difficulty of a very serious ' nature which the Agnostic Evolutionist must take into account. Some authorities maintain that certain of the anthropoid apes are higher in the scale of intelligence ' than some of the inmates of asylums, or than some of the aboriginal inhabitants of the Pacific Ocean. Now, if man is permitted to shoot the monkey and the ape, why should he not take the same liberty with the lower members of humanity? This difficulty (and there are many others of a similar nature) must be taken into consideration by the Agnostic Evolutionists, and, should the Sage of Penketh throw any light upon the subject, his efforts are deserving of great praise.— Yours &c.,

div.head: LEARNER.
div.p: A LEARNER.
October 3rd, 1892. WHY NOT OBTAIN A "LEGAL EIG UT HOURS" WORKING DAY?

Sir,—l am sorry, that some more able penman than myself has not defended, at your request, in your issue of October Ist, the above most important movement, condemned by your Sankey Bridges correspondent " Cymro " ; who fires from his concealment under the pretence of goodwill, and friendship, on all those poor struggling victims, hard and over-worked miners and others. And yet, he prides himself, that he knows something of coal-getting, its difficulties and dangers. He states that he is a "colliery engine-wright," and has fitted several hauling engines and pumps underground ; has witnessed two explosions underground,with six men killed each time. "The moan and the wail of the widow and the fatherless, the bereaved mother and stricken sister, ring in my ears, and bring tho tear to my cheek, when I think of it, although more than forty years have come and gone since then. I knew the men and their families and sympathised with them. since then many a respected neighbour and friend has gone to his account from the coal pit." It appears a little strong to one like myself, having had many narrow escapes during 30 years as a miner and an official, who has been in such terrible calamities, witnessed too many of them, and sought the living amongst the dead ; to find that men possessed of such fine moral sentiments as " Cyrnro ' displays in the above pathetic description, should now oppose, simply on the mere base £ s. d. ground, a legal measure highly calculated to mitigate the hardships and dangers, and to improve the health, the intellect, and the social and moral tone of the op- pressed producers of the world's wealth and comfort. Why should they who sink the shaft, hew the mines, plough the land, reap the harvest, temper the clay,make the bricks, mix the mortar, build the furnaces, smelt ores to make the tools, and use them in the construction ef the world's mighty machinery; by which many are mangled to death while spinning the silks and satins for the soft-handed drones of mankind, and shoddies and sackcloth for the honest producers of all the covering and raiment of the otherwise naked human world; tell me why should they who build the splendid mansions, halls, and palaces of the great do-nothings, continue to eke out their weary nights with aching over-taxed limbs in cheerless hovels that the rich would be horror- struck to take their hounds and hacks to for nightly shel- ter?"ls the world getting more lazy"(cmnpla isis"Cy mro") " than formerly? Jack wants to be as good as his master, or a little better." Jack has been good enough to risk his life in getting more and better coals to warm his master's grand mansion than his own damp malo- dorous den : good enough to cause mother earth to yield her finest products, which Jack reaped and cooked, and smilingly placed on his master's table ; which Jack also made more splendid than his own table, too often thinly sprinkled with the crumbs from his rich and bloated master's. Jack's long sufferings have opened mental eyes, and he sees that, as Carlyle says, "He that will not work according to his faculty, let him perish according to his necessity " : there is no law juster than that. Would to Heaven we could preach it abroad into the hearts of all sons and slaughters of Adam; for it is a law applicable to alt." Jack knows when he's hurt; his ill-fed, ill-clad, ill- boused, mortal, tired tabernacle, leads its immortal God-given tenant, the soul to rejoice that be has long And nobly sustained the first law of nature, if Jack is daily drinking in the knowledge that his "God is no respecter of persons " : but principles: bad law-makers are the foes of God and mankind, and therefore mist give place to better laws, &c. As every artist dips his brush in his own soul, and paints it in his pictures, so we row clearly see that hitherto the law-makers of this lower world have largely based their enactments on ,deadly selfishness, tyranny, and vain-glory. £ s. d. has tbeen the central element, and even-handed justice only the accidental. Let " Cymro " think deeper, than taunting "Jack for wanting to be as good as his master, or a little better." Jack's discontent is deep-rooted, long-lived, and mighty with the strength of justice, for shorter working hours, better remuneration. brighter and healthier homes, higher mental and moral culture, all essential to save rack—the toiling masses—from seek- ing relief bv consuming "liquid madness" (drink)" sold at tenpelce the quartern, all the products of which are and must he, like its origin, mad, miserable, ruinous, and that only," as Carlyle soundly states.—Yonrs, R. STOREY. Warrington, October 11th, 1892.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

Sir,—The Municipal Elections being close at hand, I wish to draw the atteniton of the leaders of the Liberal Party to the necessity of selecting a Catholic candidate. The Conservatives do it, and why should not the Liberals who always seek their aid? If I may be allowed to sug- gest one, I would say the President of the League of the Cross. He is a popular young man among the Catholics, and would be a great help on the School Attendance Committee.
Thanking you in anticipation,—l remain, yours &c..
A LIBERAL.
MR. ARTHUR CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.

Slr,—Should M'arrington want another Liberal candi- date some few years hence, I do not think it will have the slightest difficulty in obtaining one, and one of dis- tinctly local connection. Mr. Arthur Crosfield is the man. Be is only about 27 years ef age, and I think if one may judge from his recent speech at the Cemetery Inn, it may safely be assumed that he will be a man of remarkable eloquence in the not far distant future. His speech delivered at so out of the way a place as the comparatively obscure inn I have mentioned, ought ,to ' make that place famous in Warrington annals as the spot where was delivered one of the finest local addresses that have appeared in our press. The ability, the culture, the broad enlightened spirit, the high tone that character- ised it, were most striking, and truly refreshing in the midst of the deplorable dearth of this sort of thing which prevails in Warrington ; aye, and! might say, speaking in a comparative sense, throughout the country too. One could never have dreamt that a simple bowling match among a few workmen, would have been the occas'on of so really fine and imposing a deliverance as that of Mr. A. Crosfield. While I believe he will follow worthily in the footsteps of his father, in the industry with which they are connected, I cannot but consider that he was cut out for even better things than the carrying on of a career of soap manufacture. And in these eulogistic remarks I am by no means using metaphorically any of the saponaceous commodity with which his firm is so closely identified. Mr. Arthur Crosfield stands now more prominently before the town than ever as the rising hope of Warrington Liberalism.— Yours truly, MANLIUS. THE OUTBREAK OF SMALLPDX—AND THE

div.head: DOINGS OF OUR SANITARY CURMITTEE.
div.p: DOINGS OF OUR SANITARY CURMITTEE.

Sir,—Having read the report of the above Com- mittee's doings, and the lively doings at the Council meeting on Tuesday woek, I was somewhat surprised that one-man government should continue to exist in the management of our sanitary arrangements. We learn now, almost at the eleventh hour, that the Sub-Com- mittee in connection with the above has met once since November last. That speaks sufficiently, however, without going into this further at present. May I ask the authorities what are the best remedies for the public to adopt to assist in stamping out this epidemic ? I noticed one statement by Councillor Dr. Cannell, where he asked the Chairman of theSanitery Committee whether they had considered the necessity of ' closing our public schools, as he knew 40 cases at houses where he had been called, and the children of such are attending our day schools. I failed to see any reply to such an important question. Now, as a parent, might I suggest that an effort be made to close them, and give them all a free grant; other- wise it would be a serious loss to our schools. 'his course I consider is all the more important as the Chairman, Aldermaa Burgess, said our Medical Officer did not expect to get rid of the ephlemic of smallpox within six months. Now, as one who is called upon to visit hundreds of houses every week, might I suggest, as our sanitary officers cannot visit everyw here at once, that someone be appointed to each ward, to visit every yard, &c. irrespective of persons, and report thereon. This would only take a short time to do, but its effect would be wonderful, I am sure. Where the whitewash brush and disinfectants are required, send out men (not councillors as was suggested by the sub-committee) to do the work, and charge the landlords for doing it, which would in turn, stir them up with the tenant, and thus they would be kept clean. The watering carts and hosepipe might visit our back streets to swill and cleanse where pure water is a stranger, except when it rains.—l remain, yours, &c., _ _ _
COLLECTOR.
THE EIGHT HOURS LEGAL DAT.

Sir,—You kindly inserted in your valuable paper a letter from me on the subject of an " eight hours legal day." lam in hopes that some of your correspondents or readers who have studied the question will favour the uninstructed like myself, with some explanation as to the modus operandi by which it is to be accomplished. With all due deference to the leaders of the movement, who shout for a universal legal day of eight hours— compelling all men, and women too, to cease working every day when eight hours' work has been got through, I contend that in a vast number, in fact in the majority, of cases, it is impracticable.

The great bulk of our manufacturers of textile fabrics, linen, woollen, cotton, hardware of all descriptions, iron. steel, copper, tin, chemicals, and nearly all classes of goods—have to find a market otherwhere than in this country. We have to contend with hostile tariffs, and with workmen who work longer hours for less wages. Don't let it be supposed that I am hostile to the move- ment. I shall be glad to see it succeed ; but what I want is information, same tangible plan as to its work- ing out satisfactorily alike to employers and employed. We have a legal day now for women and children and young persons in factories; but how much further can we go ? Shopkeepers can be compelled to work their assistants only so many hours a day; but how about the smaller trades and indus,ries. Many trades do not get their work to commence the week with until Tuesday ; Monday is lost in waiting, and in order to get anything like a week's wage, extra wort must be done between then and Saturday to make good to some extent, lost time. Must this extra time worked be treated as crime or misdemeanor?

Supposing an epidemic such as the present smallpox or cholera break out, and people die at an abnormal and extraordipary rate ? Must the undertaker stop at eight' hours? Do those tradesmen keep ready-made graves and coffins? Or do they supply these necessaries as the cases arise ? I don't think eight hours will work here. Who then shall work eight hours and who shall not? What class of labour shall be bound down, and what class free? Some trades and occupations lose much time in winteri and had weather, often getting in arrears with rent and often for food and common necessaries—shall not the fine weather and long days' of summer, with work , plentiful, be taken advantage of, to rub off this encum- brance of debt ; and, if possible, lay a little aside for a future rainy day—without being guilty of felmy ? Let each trade fix its own hours by a combination among themselves—making its own rules arid excep- tions. I can't see that the shoemakers save any right to legislate for the masons, or the bricklayers for the tailors. Slack times will come; they are with us now— and men by thousands are involuntarily idle. It is to be hoped that busy times will come again, and soon, to compensate in 80[110 degree for past depression. I think the labour leaders, wh ) shout for eight hours, study more to tell their hearers what they would like to hear, rather than endeavour to teach them what is practical and practicable, and what can be achieved, and and what can not, where an eight hours day will work, and where it will not. I cannot see how the great army of casuals can be brought under any organization, as to any number of hours. I leave it to those who know better, and hope soon to know from some quarter more on this subject than I do, and thousands besides me. I look at it in this way ; there are eight men at cer- tain works this week; they have been last week and have been for perhaps years. They have worked 9 hours per day during all that time; next week and in future they work 8 hours a day. Will they do the same amount of work in the 8 hours they did in the 9 hours day ? Or must an extra hand be taken on to accomplish the same? How about the wages? If 9 men are employed instead of 8, will the 8 sacrifice 121 per cent. of their former earnings to pay the 9th man? Or must the employer Day that much more in wages ? Or must the price of the article in the market be advanced to that amount ? I anxiously wait a satisfactory answer to these questions r—lst harder work in the time ; 2nd an extra hand at 121 per cent., more cost ; 3rd or 121 per cent, increased price in the market. How is it to be ? I am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO. Sankey Bridges, October sth, 1892.

div.head: SUPPOSED WRECK AND LOSS OF 40 LIVES.
div.p: SUPPOSED WRECK AND LOSS OF 40 LIVES.

The Boulogne correspondent of the "Daily News," writing on Tuesday night, says :—The captain of the French sloop Jean Bap:iste, from Portsmouth, which arrived here on Monday, has reported to the Commissary of Marine having passed from 35 to 40 dead bodies and a large number of cases in white wood floating on the surface of the water about two miles off Saint Valery sur Somme, between one and three on Sunday morning. The gale was then at its height and the sloop running before it. Some of the bodies wee dressed in nil skins, but the rest were not in sailors' dress. The other two men of the sloop confirm this statement,but believe that the number nf bodies was much greater. The Commis- sary has addressed inquiries to the difbrent stations along the coast.

A telegram from Yarmouth states that it has now been ascertained that the vessel wrecked on Hasbro Sands last Tuesday was the Danish schooner Samlot, bound for France with ice. Four of the crew were drowned, the captain and one seaman being taken off frcm the floating wreckage by a boat from the Woold Lightship.

div.head: INSANI I'A.RY AREA IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE INSANI I'A.RY AREA IN WARRINGTON.
IMPORTANT REPORT.
SHOCKING REVELATIONS.

1 As our readers are aware, Or. Gprnall, medical officer of health, has several times in the past direc- ted the attention of the Sanitary Committee of the I Town Council to the insanitary area in the neigh- bourhood of Cockhedge, which is exceptionally bad. lie prepared a special report upon the subject, which was submitted to the Sanitary Committee, and, following upon that, a resolution was passed in February by the Town Council, and directed the Medical Officer and Mr. horrgdin, the borough surveyor, to prepare a report conjointly. The reso- lution on the subject was as fonows : That a report be prepared showing the houses, courts, and alleys that are (1) Fit for human habitation ; (2) Unfit, but capable of being mode fit for humani habitation ; _ _ . .

(3) Unfit, and incapable of being made fit for human habitation ; and also showing in what manner it is proposed to improve the said area so as to remedy the sanitary defects in such area ; ; That the Medical Officer of Health and the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare such report, and that they be authorized to obtain such assistance as they may require for such purpose ; That the Medical Officer of Health prepare an analysis of the death-rate during the last five years, showing the ages and causes of mortality in the said area ; In accordance with these instructions the two officers of the Corporation got to work and prepared a report and submitted it to the Sanitary Committee as far back as April last. It has been a matter for wonder to those who have been interested in this matter, that the report has not been submitted to the Town Council. It is dated April 28th, 1892, and October has been reached without the report, so far as we can hear, being dealt with by the Sanitary Committee or laid before the Town Council. The questions which are being asked are, How is this? arni, Why is the report being kept back? We have been successful after many inquiries in obtain- ing a copy of this report, and we proceed to submit the more important portions of it to our readers, in the be- lief that the matter is one requiring urgent attention. The report is styled a '6 Sanitary survey of the condi- tion of houses bounded on the south side by Dial-st., on the north by Cockhedgenane, on the east by Fennel-st., and on the west by an imaginary line, drawn front No. 58. Cockhedge-lane, to 12, Dial-st., made by the Medical Officer of Health, and the Borough Surveyor."
It proceeds, "The area covered is about two acres, and contains within its limits 12 courts or yards, as follows :

Dial Yard Rose Yard Flag Yard Dial Court Filling's Court Webster's Yard Green's Court Vernon's Yard Pi I ki ngton's Yard Robinson's Yard Pritchard's Yard Garner's Brow And one street called Carlisle Street.

All these courts and street, with the exception of Dial Court, are cul de sacs, having only one entrance. There are 152 dwelling-houses built on the area—of which 6 are not inhabited—and occupied by 623 people. It will be noticed that there is a population of about 300 persons per acre. A modern area, such as got by property being erected with streets and passages, according to the existing Borough Bye-laws, gives a population of 200 per acre. Each house has geen thoroughly inspected, and in. many cases the houses were found so arranged that reasonable ventilation is impossible, and also, without re-construction, could not be rendered sanitary. The closet accommodation to many of the houses is inadequate." Following this are tables which give particulars ot the dwellings in each street and court separately, and also of the population. The report is accompanied by a map of the locality which shows at a glance the number of courts and yards, which are obviously closed in and supplied with neither light nor air in anything like sufficient quantities. No one can glance at the map without seeing that, as a matter of neccessity, such an area must of necessity be an unhealthy one. Below we quote some "descriptions "of the property to be met with in the various streets and yards. In Dial-st., it seems quite a usual thing for houses to have the closets in common. The closet of No. 18 is yards away and on the premises of another landlord. In the case of No 36 the closet is situated 60 yards away, and the residents use it in common with the inmates of five other houses. No 22 is separated only by 31t. Bin. from a building used as a meat-boiling room. No 28 suffers from a number of defects. Its closet is in com- mon with other houses, it has no slop stone, the eaves and downspouting are defective, causing dampness, and the outside brickwork is very open in the joints. In Fennel-st., the closet of one house is as far as 100 feet ' away, while in another it is as near the back of , the house as 21t. lin. One house does not boast a yard, while another is accommAated with a cow-house for ten Cows, and a large manure heap adjacent. There is a closet in close proximity to a bakehouse, and there are windows which do not open. One house in Cockhedge-lane is described as follows "Ventilation bad ; no slop stone accommodation ; house very dirty, closet within 3ft. 6in. of back door," and this is a dis- cription which applies to several other habitations. In another case thorugh ventilation cannot be obtained, except by knocking two houses into one, and such epithets as " filthy " and " very dirty " are used with regard to some of the houses. No. 2, of Rose Yard, is said to be a" dilapidated" building, while No. 5 has the doubtful advantage of having three closets adjoining it. In Dial Court. Pilling's Court; Webster's Yard, Green's Court, Vernon's Yard, Pilkington's Yard, Robinson's Yard, Pritchard's Yard, and Garners Brow, and Flag Yard, the houses are reported upon as being in many instance, seriously defective. In Dial Court, for instance, there are closets adjoining houses, and in several cases the down-spouts and yards require repair- ing and paving. In Green's Court there are four houses to one closet, and another house has three closets within five feet of it. In addition to that all the houses In Green's Court use well water ; no town's water having been laid on. Out of the total number of houses commented noon there are no fewer than 74 without through writilation of any kind. In Flag-yard, Pllkington's-yard, Green's Court, and Web- ster's-yard. there does not aprar to be a single house that has any through ventilatioh.

From this table it will be seen that for 1890 and 1891 the death-rate in this insanitary area—this Black Spot" of Warrington—is 50 per cent above the average of the borough, an average which, it is well to bear in mind, includes this insanitary area. div.p: TENNYSON'S BURIAL.
IMPRESSIVE CEREMONY AT WEST- MIM•!Tigit ABBEYr

With a solemnity and simple impressiveness in keep- ing with the known sentirne..ts of the great poet, who so dislikethe•• trappings sad the suits of woe," the remains of Lord Tennyson were on Wednesday after- noon placed to rest in Westminster Abbey, near the tombs of ms ti ef, England's greatest singers. The an- cient Minster was thronged with a distinguished multi- tude, and thosewlio sought to do final homage to the late Laureate inci+aded the most distinguished represent- atives of state.nrisinship, art, Trecatunr, music, and science.

Shortly afterll2:o'clock the Abbey clergy, the mourn- ers, and the pallbearers assembled at the chawr doors. Dr. Bradley's indisposition was hawpily not sufficilently serious to prevent him from officiating, and with him were the Rev. Dr. Duckworth, Canorr in residence, Arch- deacon Farrar, the Rev. Flood Jones, precentor, Canon Furse, Dr. Troutbeck, and other members of the chap- ter. Following the coffin were the mourners. Among the chief mourners were Mr. and Mrs. Hallam Tenny- son, Masters Lionel and Aubrey Tennyson, Rev. W. Pope and Mrs. Pope, Mr. Ernest Boyle., Mr. and Mrs. L. Boyle, Mr. and Mrs. Cecil Boyle, Mr. A. Haibottle Estcourt, Mrs. James Baillie, Mr. Arthur and Mrs.. Tennyson, Admiral Tennyson D'Eyncourt, Mr. and Mrs. Lewis D'Eyncourt, Mr.. mid Mrs. Horatio Tennyson, Mr. and Mrs. Edmund Lushington, Miss Tennyson, Mr. Frank Lushington, Captain and Mrs. Tennyson, Mr. Alfred Tennyson, Mr; and Mrs. Arden, Miss Violet Tennyson, Mr. and Mrs. Birrell, Masters Alfred and Charles Tennyson, Mr. Walter and Mrs. IGw, Captain Arthur Jesse, Mr. and Mrs. W. Rawnsley,. Rev. Canon Wright, Mrs. and Miss -Weld, Colonel and Mrs. Ford, Mr. and Mrs. Locker Lampson, Lord and Lady Boyne, Mr. Godfrey Locker Lampson, Mr. A. Lefroy, Sir Andrew Clark, Mrs. MOrduant Boyle, Rev.: H. D. and Mrs. Rawnsley, and Mr; G. Craik. The pall, which was of transparent texture, woven at the Keswick School of Industrial Art, and embroidered with pink, roses and with the last verse of the poem, " Crossing the Bar," was borne by
The Marquis of Salisbury Sir James Paget The Duke of Argyll Master of Trinity, College, Lord Selborne .Cambridge . _
Lord Dufferirt Lord Tiosebery
Master of Dallia College, Oxford
Mr. White (United States Mr.W. E. H. Lecky. Legation) Mr. J. A, Fronde Lord Kelvin

Over all was spread a Union Jack, sent by General Lord Methuen, commanding the Home District and used in accordance with a wish expressed by Lady Tennyson, who was not present, that the coffin should be covered with a flag representing " the feeling of the beloved Queen and the nation, and the Empire he loved so • dear." The procession numbered nearly 200; and in- • cluded the Vice-chancellors of Oxford and Cambridge, . the representatives of the two Universities, and of Edin- burgh, Glasgow, Dublin, London, and Manchester, of the Royal Society, and the Royal Academy, amongst , them being Professor Huxley, -Sir John Lubbock, Sir John Evans, Dr. Michael Foster,Sir Archibald Geikie,Mr. Norman Lockyer, the Archbishops of Canterbury and York, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, M.P., and Mr. Bryce, M.P., together with representatives of the other branch—the Tennyson-d'Eyncourts—.f the family. Not the least conspicuous amongst the mourners were 200 lads from the Gordon Boys' Home, in whioh Lord Tennyson took a deep interest, and who were allotted places- in the nave. .

Some time prior to thisthe solemn hush which had pre- vailed in the Abbey was broken by the majestic- strains of the death march, "In Memory of a Great Man," from Beethoven's " Erorica " symphony, played on the organ by Dr. Bridge. A brief interval followed, and then the vast congregation rose simultaneously as the organ pealed forth the music of Purcell and Croft's setting of the' Opening sentences of the Burial Service, which the choir was heard chanting in the distance. Slowly and. with stately movement the procession wended its way into the Abbey, and up the nave, and at this supreme mo- ment there was, perhaps, not a person in the building whose feelings were irresponsive to the pathos, the dignity, the noble simplicity of the ceremony in which they had the privilege of taking part. The Ninetieth Ps t Im was sung by the Abbey choir to Purcell's chant in G,and the interment music was that of Croft. Of course the chief interest with regard to the music centred in the two anthems, " Crossing the Bar," composed by Dr. Bridge, and another to 12 unfinished lines, entitled" The Silent Voices," by the poet, which have been set to music by Lady Tennyson, and arranged by Dr. Bridge. It Ii a beautiful and scholarly work, and was rendered with wonderful expressiveness by the choir, most par- ticularly the last verse, which breathes such trust and hopefulness : For though from forth this bourne of time and space, The flood may bear me far. I know that I shall see my Pilot face to face When I have crossed the bar. The second anthem is arranged as a four-part chorus with organ accompaniment, in F minor and F majnr, the passages in the minor being of an extremely dirge- like character, which give place to more jubilant strains in the major key. In every respect the music of the.two compositions was worthy of the place and the occasion, and will add lustre to the memories of the day. Chopin's "March Funebre "was played as the body was carried to the grave: and here, by express wish of Lady Tenny- son Bishop Heber's hyme "Holy, holy, holy,,Lord God Almighty," set to Dr. Dyke's music, was sung, this being a favourite hymn with the deceased Laureate. There was no sermon, and with the benediction pronounced by the Dean, the touching ceremony came to an end, hut the great bulk of the congregation did net leave the building until Ike last echoes had died away of the Dead March from " Saul," which was played by Dr.. Btidge, while everybody stood. The floral offerings sent were almost innumerable. They not only covered the great table in the Jerusalem Chamber, but the floor as well, to such an e.-etent, indeed, that there was scarcely space to move. Two wreaths were sent by the Queen, just before the burial ceremony andldeposited at the peed of the grave. One, which was of natural laurel, bore a card inscribed, in her Majesty's own handwriting, the inscription, " A mark of sincere regard and admiration from Victoria, R. 1." Another which was sent by her Majesty was of laurel in metal, and was inscribed, " A tribute of affec- tionate regard and true admiration from his Sovereign." At the grave-head also was deposited a wreath of white flowers as" A mark of respect from Princess Beatrice." From the wife of the Prime Minister. came a wreath of ferns, to which Mrs. Gladstone attached the lines— "leave him There in the vast Cathedral; God accept him, Christ receive htrn." A memorial service took place in the Parish Church, Freshwater, simultaneously r with the funeral of Lord Tennyson. The work of filling in the grave et the Laureate was commenced Immediately after the elosin,g of the Abbey doers on Wednesday evening, and by Thursday morn- ing. the task was completed, and the stone slab retursted tots place. The beautiful pall worked at Keswick has been laid over the stone, and at the head of the grave has been placed a magnificent cross,some four feet high, composed of white flowers and violets' surmounted on one arm by a white dove. The wreaths and other floral tributes are now lying round the grave, which has been railed off as a protection against the crowds visiting the Abbey. TENNYSONIANA. A London rector writes :—A visitor of the poet yen, tured so ask him what he thought of our Lord Jesus Christ. They were walking in dee garden, and for a , minute he said nothing : then he stopped by some beau- fill flower, and said simply What the sun is to that flower, Jesus Christ is to my soul. He is the Sun of my soul." When his son asked him during his last illness,from his mother, how he felt, he opened it volume of Shakspeare, containing " Cymbeline," half unconsciously at the page containing the words— Haile there like fruit my soul Till the tree die. He had been wont to call it "the tenderest repartee," if you may call it so, in "Shakspeare." His last words, except those of blessing to Lady Tennyson and his son, were, "I have opened the book." - The news that the copy of Shakspeare which Tenny- son read on his death-bed has been buried with him re- calls a pleasant story of a dinner party at Aldworth, at which the merits of English poets were being hotly dis- cussed. Some declared for Wordsworth, others for Shelley, others for Byron. The host alone sat silent. At length he burst out, The whole lot of 'em won't match Shakspeare."

One of the degrees issued by the Queen Regent of Spain in referenci to the Columbus celebration appoints the 12th nr October to be a national holiday for ever. In America and Spain the celebrations on Wednesday, were of an enthusiastic character. .

A tt. Petersburg telegram states that according to official returns a quarter ot a million people have died of cholera throughout Russia this year. The remains of Mr. Thomas Woolner, R.A the famous sculptor, were on Thursday interred at Headed Old Parish Church, some eight talks from London.
